title: Acceptance
summary: The learnable capacity to let painful emotions, thoughts and unchangeable facts be what they are, noticing them without judging or fighting them, so that energy goes to what still matters and can still be done. It is not approval of what happened, and not resignation.
selfCheck: Am I fighting a feeling I'm entitled to have, or criticising myself for having it?
Is this situation truly fixed, or am I calling it unchangeable so I don't have to act?
Am I accepting what happened, or am I approving of it or giving up?
Once I've let this be, what is the one step that still matters most?

example.situation: A week before a product launch, a team lead learns that a key engineer is leaving and the launch date cannot move.
example.before: I shouldn't be this rattled; I'm the lead. I'll push the worry down, tell everyone it's fine, and keep reopening the decision to let her go in my head all weekend.
example.after: I'm anxious and a bit hurt, and that makes sense the week before a launch. The departure is settled. What's still open is the handover and which features we cut, so that's where this afternoon goes.
example.why: The wiser response stops spending effort on fighting the feeling and the fact, which leaves attention free for the parts of the situation that can still be shaped; it accepts the departure without giving up on the launch.

title: Adversity
summary: The situation of meeting serious hardship, such as illness, job loss, divorce, failure or other misfortune that cannot simply be avoided. Wisdom here means bearing the pain without adding needless suffering to it, acting on what is still in one's power, and later reflecting on the experience openly rather than forcing a tidy lesson from it.
selfCheck: Am I adding a "second arrow" of blame, catastrophe or self-pity to the pain this situation actually brings?
Which parts of this are up to me right now, and which are not?
When I look back on this, am I trying to understand what happened and what it taught me, or only to tie it up neatly?
Is the load more than I can carry alone, so that it is time to lean on others or talk to a professional?

example.situation: A team lead learns that the product she spent two years building is being cancelled and her role will end in three months.
example.before: This is a disaster and it's unfair. I'll replay every meeting tonight to find who's to blame, and tell everyone I'm totally fine.
example.after: This really hurts, and I don't have to pretend otherwise. I can't change the decision, but I can update my CV, talk to two mentors this week and tell my partner how I'm feeling. In a few months I'll look back at what I'd do differently, not just at how to feel better about it.
example.why: Separating the loss itself from the stories piled on top of it, acting on what is still controllable and leaning on others protects judgment, and open, exploratory reflection afterwards is the kind linked to wisdom.

title: After-action review
summary: A short, structured, non-punitive conversation held soon after a task or event, in which the people who did the work establish what was supposed to happen, what actually happened, why, and what they will keep or change next time, so that experience turns into judgment instead of blame or forgetting.
selfCheck: Am I looking at what happened in order to learn from it, or to find someone to blame, including myself?
Have I heard how this looked to the other people involved before deciding why it went the way it did?
Did I ask what went right and why, or only what went wrong?
What is the one concrete thing I will do differently next time, and when will I check that I did it?
steps: Hold the review soon after the event, while memories are fresh, and keep it short; for a long project, review at each milestone rather than only at the end.
Agree at the start that the purpose is learning, not grading or blame, and that what is said will not be used to punish anyone.
Establish what was supposed to happen, using the original plan, goals or standards.
Reconstruct what actually happened from several viewpoints and from any objective records, before anyone explains or defends.
Ask why the gap opened, looking for specific causes you could influence, including your own decisions.
Review what went well and why, not only what went wrong.
Agree on one to three concrete things to sustain or change, name who will apply each, and check at the start of the next similar task that they were applied.

example.situation: A small team's bid for a client contract has just been turned down, two weeks after an intense push to finish the proposal.
example.before: The manager sends a one-line message blaming the client's budget, the team moves straight to the next bid, and nobody mentions that the pricing section was finished in a rush on the last night.
example.after: The manager books thirty minutes the next morning, says the aim is to learn rather than to find fault, and asks what the plan was, what actually happened and why. The team notices that the scope was settled late and the pricing was never reviewed, also notes that the client praised the case studies, and agrees that next time pricing gets a review two days before the deadline, with one person responsible.
example.why: A specific, blame-free look at both what worked and what failed turns a disappointment into a lesson the team will actually use, instead of a convenient external excuse or a quiet repeat of the same mistake.

title: Amor fati
summary: Nietzsche's ideal of "love of fate": wanting nothing about one's life to have been different and learning not merely to bear what is necessary, including loss and hardship, but to affirm it as part of a life one can say yes to.
selfCheck: Am I spending my energy wishing this had not happened, or deciding what to make of the fact that it did?
Am I calling something "fate" to avoid changing what I could and should still change?
Could I tell the story of this setback as part of a life I would still choose to live again?

example.situation: A project manager's carefully planned product launch is cancelled after a reorganisation, and months of her team's work will never ship.
example.before: This should never have happened. I keep replaying the meeting where it was killed and resenting everyone in it, and I've stopped caring about the next project.
example.after: It happened, and it is now part of my story and the team's. What did these months teach us, and what can we carry into the next thing? I'll grieve it honestly, then decide what to build from it.
example.why: The wiser response neither pretends the loss was good nor fights the fact that it occurred; it takes the event as given and asks what a life that includes it can become.

title: Aristotle
summary: Greek philosopher (384–322 BCE), student of Plato and founder of the Lyceum, whose ethics gave the West its most influential account of practical wisdom (phronesis): the experienced, character-based judgment that sees what a particular situation calls for, built up through habit and aimed at a flourishing life (eudaimonia).

title: Balance theory of wisdom
summary: Robert Sternberg's model of wisdom as the use of intelligence, creativity, knowledge and experience, guided by positive ethical values, to reach a common good by balancing one's own, other people's and wider interests over the short and long term, and by choosing well among adapting to a situation, reshaping it or leaving it.
selfCheck: Whose interests have I left off the list, including people who are not in the room?
Would this choice still look good to me a year from now, not just this week?
Am I adapting, trying to change things, or walking away, and is that the right response here?
Is the common good I am appealing to one the other people affected would recognise, or just my own preference dressed up?
steps: Name the decision and the outcome you are tempted to choose before you start weighing it.
List the interests at stake on three levels - yours, those of the specific people around you, and those of the wider team, community or environment.
For each option, write down who gains and who pays in the next few weeks and in a few years.
Ask whether to adapt to the situation, try to change it, or leave it for a better one, and why.
Choose the option that best serves a common good you could defend out loud to everyone affected, and say which value settled the trade-off.

example.situation: A team lead is offered a high-profile project that would mean handing a struggling junior colleague's half-finished work to someone else three days before the client deadline.
example.before: This is my shot. Take the project, reassign the work tonight and let the junior person sort themselves out.
example.after: I want this project, the junior colleague needs support, and the client needs the deliverable. Can I ask for a one-week start date, pair them with a senior for three days, and take the project after?
example.why: The first answer serves only one interest in the short term; the second looks for an option that balances personal, interpersonal and wider interests over a longer horizon, which is what Sternberg means by a wise solution.

title: Berlin wisdom paradigm
aliases: wisdom as expertise in the fundamental pragmatics of life
summary: A research model, developed by Paul Baltes and colleagues in Berlin, that treats wisdom as expert knowledge and judgment about the conduct and meaning of life, measured by rating people's think-aloud answers to hard life dilemmas against five criteria.
selfCheck: Have I considered how this problem looks across the person's whole life, past and future, and not only today?
Have I named what I do not know about this situation, and what I would do if things turn out differently than I expect?
Am I judging this choice by my own values only, or have I tried to understand the values and priorities behind it?

title: Bhagavad Gita
summary: A Sanskrit dialogue set in Book VI of the Mahabharata, probably composed around the first or second century CE, in which Krishna answers the warrior Arjuna's moral paralysis before battle with teachings on acting without attachment to results, on one's own duty, on steady wisdom and equanimity, and on knowledge and devotion.
selfCheck: Am I doing this because it is the right thing for me to do here, or only for what I hope to get from it?
If the result goes against me, will I still be able to say I acted well?
Is my calm steadiness, or have I quietly stopped caring about the people my action affects?

example.situation: A project lead has spent months on a proposal that goes to a review board next week, and a promotion may ride on the board's verdict.
example.before: Everything depends on their yes. I'll cut the risky analysis they might question, and if they say no, the whole year was wasted.
example.after: My part is to make this proposal as sound and honest as I can, including the analysis they might question. I want a yes, but I'll judge my work by whether I did it well, not only by what the board decides.
example.why: The wiser response keeps caring about the outcome while letting the quality of the action, which is in your hands, guide what you do, which is close to what the Gita's teaching on the fruits of action asks.

title: Buddhism
summary: A religious and philosophical tradition that began with the teaching of Siddhārtha Gautama, the Buddha, in northern India around the fifth century BCE, which diagnoses suffering as arising from craving and ignorance and sets out a path of ethics, meditation and wisdom to bring it to an end.

title: Cardinal virtues
summary: The classical grouping of four virtues on which a good character was said to hinge: practical wisdom (prudence), justice, courage (fortitude) and temperance (moderation). First set out as the virtues of a well-ordered city and soul in Plato's Republic, it was taken up by the Stoics, Cicero and Christian moral theology, where it gained the name "cardinal", from the Latin cardo, hinge.
selfCheck: What do I actually know here, and what am I only assuming or hoping?
What do I owe each person affected, including the people who are not in the room?
Is fear of discomfort stopping me from doing what I already judge to be right?
Is appetite, anger or the wish to look good pushing me past the right measure?
Am I leaning hard on one virtue, such as boldness or caution, at the expense of the others?

example.situation: Your director asks you to present quarterly figures to the board with a forecast you believe is unrealistically rosy. Several colleagues' jobs depend on the board approving the plan.
example.before: Either keep quiet because it isn't my call, or stand up in the board meeting and announce that the numbers are fudged.
example.after: Check what the data actually support, raise the concern privately with the director first with the evidence and an honest alternative framing, and escalate calmly if it is ignored.
example.why: Silence fails courage and justice, while a public outburst is courage without prudence or temperance. Asking all four questions together (what is true, what is owed, what must be faced, what is the right measure) produces a response that is honest, fair, brave and proportionate at once, which is the point of treating the virtues as a set.

title: Classification of desires
summary: Epicurus's teaching that desires are natural and necessary, natural but unnecessary, or empty (born of groundless opinion), and that a good life comes from meeting the first, enjoying the second lightly, and seeing through the third, whose objects can never be had in full.
selfCheck: Would going without this actually cause me pain, or would I just feel I had fallen behind someone?
Does this desire have a natural stopping point, or would more always seem better?
What am I already giving up, in time, health or peace, to chase it?

example.situation: After a good year, a project manager starts eyeing a bigger house, a premium car and a more senior title, and finds herself working weekends and sleeping badly to get all three.
example.before: Everyone at my level has these things. Once I have them I'll finally be able to relax.
example.after: Which of these would actually hurt to go without? We need more space for the kids, so that's real. The car and the title are mostly about how I look next to others, and I can drop them if they cost my evenings.
example.why: Sorting the wants separates a real need from desires driven by comparison, so effort goes where it buys security and the rest stops dictating her time.

title: Cognitive defusion
summary: A practice from acceptance and commitment therapy for stepping back from a painful or unhelpful thought and seeing it as a passing string of words rather than a literal truth or an order, without arguing with it or trying to make it go away, so that it has less grip on what you do next.
selfCheck: Am I treating this thought as a fact about the world, or as something my mind is saying right now?
Is this thought helping me act on what matters here, or just making me want to escape?
Am I using a defusion trick to make the feeling go away, rather than to make room for it?
Have I checked whether the thought is pointing to a real problem that deserves action?
steps: Notice when a thought is steering you, especially a harsh verdict about yourself or a prediction of disaster that you are treating as plain fact.
Name it as a thought by restating it as "I'm having the thought that…", or label its kind, such as "the not-good-enough story" or "a prediction".
Loosen its literal hold for a few seconds by saying its key word aloud quickly and repeatedly, or saying the sentence very slowly or in a silly voice, until it sounds more like sounds than a message.
Let it stay without arguing with it, proving it wrong or pushing it away; acknowledge it, for example by thanking your mind for the warning.
Ask what you would do next if this thought were just background noise, and take that step while the thought comes along.
Stop and seek professional support if a thought is overwhelming, persistent or about harming yourself; defusion is a self-help skill, not crisis care.

example.situation: Ten minutes before presenting a proposal to senior leaders, a manager keeps hearing the thought "they're going to see I'm out of my depth".
example.before: It's true, I'm out of my depth. I'll trim the proposal to the safe parts, skip the risky recommendation and read straight from the slides so nobody can ask me anything.
example.after: I'm having the thought that they'll see I'm out of my depth. That's the old not-good-enough story turning up before a big meeting, as it usually does. It can come along; I'll still make the recommendation I believe in and take the questions.
example.why: The wiser response neither obeys the thought nor wastes the last ten minutes trying to argue it away; seeing it as a familiar mental event leaves the manager free to act on the judgement they actually hold.

title: Cognitive reappraisal
summary: Changing how you interpret an emotional situation, what it means, how you look at it or what it implies, so that its emotional impact changes, rather than changing the situation itself or hiding what you feel.
selfCheck: Is this something I can still change, so that I should act rather than reinterpret?
Is my new reading of the situation true, or just comfortable?
Am I using a reframe to talk myself out of a feeling that is telling me something important, such as that I'm being treated unfairly?
Did the reframe actually change how I feel, or do I need a different approach?
steps: Name the feeling and the specific thought driving it, for example "I'm anxious because I think this mistake will get me fired."
Ask whether you can still change the situation itself; if you can, plan that action first and use reappraisal only to steady yourself enough to act.
Test the interpretation against the facts, as you would a colleague's claim, and look for what you actually know versus what you are assuming.
Try one or two alternative readings that are also true, such as what the event will matter in a year, what you can still influence, or how a neutral observer would describe it.
Pick the reading you can honestly believe, not the most comforting one, and let it guide your next step.
After a while, check whether the feeling has shifted; if the reframe isn't landing, switch to another strategy such as acceptance, talking it through or taking a break.

example.situation: A project lead learns in a meeting that the client has rejected the proposal their team spent three weeks on.
example.before: This is a disaster and it proves I'm not good at this. I'll just smile, say it's fine, and stew about it tonight.
example.after: This stings, and it's a real setback. What do I actually know? They rejected this version, not the team. Some of it I can still change: I'll ask for their reasons tomorrow. The part I can't change I'll treat as one lost bid in a long year, not a verdict on us.
example.why: The wiser response keeps the feeling honest, uses reappraisal on the part that can't be changed, and keeps the frustration that should drive action on the part that can, instead of masking everything and ruminating later.

title: Common wisdom model
summary: A 2020 consensus framework from an international task force of wisdom scientists that defines wisdom as metacognition applied to reasoning and problem-solving and grounded in morality: perspectival metacognition (knowing the limits of one's knowledge, weighing several viewpoints, adapting to context) joined to moral aspirations (pursuit of truth, prosocial goals, a sense of shared humanity).
selfCheck: What do I not know about this situation, and how might the facts change what I think?
Whose perspective have I not yet considered, and what would this look like from where they stand?
Is there a way forward that serves both my interests and theirs, rather than one at the other's expense?
Am I aiming at what is true and fair here, or only at winning the point?

title: Compassion
summary: The settled disposition to notice another's suffering, be moved by it without being overwhelmed, and want and act to relieve it, steered by judgement about what will actually help.
selfCheck: Have I actually noticed what this person is going through, or only what their trouble costs me?
Am I acting to ease their suffering, or to escape my own discomfort at seeing it?
Is my concern shaded by a quiet judgement that they brought this on themselves, or that I am above them?
Would I feel and act the same way if the people suffering were many, distant or unlike me?

example.situation: A reliable team member misses a client deadline and, when you ask about it, mentions that a parent was taken into hospital last week.
example.before: I either brush past it ('sorry to hear that, but the client is furious, I need it by tomorrow') or I am so upset for them that I quietly redo the work myself at midnight and never mention the deadline again.
example.after: I stop and take it in: 'That's a hard week. What would help most right now?' I move the deadline with the client myself, ask whether they want work taken off them or kept as a distraction, and agree a check-in for next week so the rest of the team isn't left guessing.
example.why: Compassion notices the suffering and is moved by it, but it also stays steady enough to choose help that fits this person and stays fair to everyone else involved.

title: Compassionate reappraisal
aliases: letting go of anger through compassion
summary: A short reflective exercise for someone who has wronged you: you keep the wrong in view but deliberately see the offender as a whole, flawed human being who needs to change, and try to wish them well, instead of replaying the hurt.
selfCheck: Am I wishing this person well, or am I telling myself that what they did was fine?
Is this wrong still going on and within my power to change, so that action rather than reappraisal is the priority?
After the exercise, what concrete step, if any, does fairness to me or others still require?
Am I trying this because I'm ready, or because I feel I ought to have moved on by now?
steps: Sit somewhere quiet and settle your breathing for a minute or two before you start.
Recall one specific time a particular person hurt or wronged you, and name plainly what they did and what it cost you.
Picture the offender as a whole person with a history, fears and other sides to them, not only as the author of this act.
Treat the wrong as a sign that this person needs to grow or change, without telling yourself it was acceptable.
Try, for about two minutes, to sincerely wish them something good, such as healing or becoming someone who would not do this again.
Notice your thoughts, feelings and body as you do this, and repeat the exercise when you catch yourself replaying the hurt.
Decide separately, on the facts, what boundary, conversation or accountability the situation still needs.

example.situation: A teammate missed a handover deadline and then told your manager the delay was your fault, and you lie awake replaying it.
example.before: I keep going over every word they said to the manager. They're two-faced, that's all there is to it, and I'll be cold to them from now on.
example.after: They were wrong to blame me, and I'll correct the record with the manager tomorrow. They were scared of being blamed, which doesn't excuse it, and I hope they learn to own their mistakes. I can wish them that and still watch my back.
example.why: Replaying the offence keeps anger and arousal high, while seeing the person as flawed and in need of change lets the anger ease without denying the wrong or giving up the practical response.

title: Confucianism
summary: The East Asian tradition of thought and practice that grew from the teaching of Confucius (Kong Qiu, 551–479 BCE), which holds that a good life and a good society come from lifelong learning and self-cultivation, expressed through humaneness (ren), ritual propriety (li), care for family and the example of the exemplary person (junzi).

title: Contentment
summary: The settled sense that one's present life is sufficient and complete as it is, together with the habit of not letting limitless wanting set the terms of one's peace; a quiet, low-arousal good rather than an excited one.
selfCheck: If nothing changed tomorrow, would my life be enough, and what exactly would be missing?
Is this want mine, or did a comparison or an advert just switch it on?
Have I confused being content with giving up on something that genuinely needs fixing?
When I last got what I wanted, how long did the satisfaction actually last?

example.situation: A colleague in a similar role announces a promotion and a bigger title, and your own job, which you liked yesterday, suddenly feels small.
example.before: I need to start interviewing elsewhere this week; I can't be the one who got left behind.
example.after: Is anything about my work actually worse than it was yesterday? If there's something I really want, like the scope or the pay, I'll go after that on purpose. If not, I'll let the comparison pass.
example.why: Contentment separates a real, specific need from wanting that was switched on by comparison; it keeps ambition but stops it from setting the price of one's peace.

title: Courage
summary: The character trait of facing real risk, fear or loss for the sake of something worth protecting or doing, with fear and confidence in proportion to what is actually at stake; in the classical view it is a mean between cowardice and rashness that needs practical wisdom to tell a worthy risk from a foolish one.
selfCheck: What exactly am I afraid of losing here, and is that fear in proportion to the real stakes?
Is the cause worth the risk I am about to take, or am I mainly after looking brave?
If I stay silent, is that a judgment about timing, or am I just avoiding discomfort?
Have I prepared, framed and planned the follow-up, or am I acting on a surge of anger?

example.situation: In a planning meeting, a senior director presents a launch date that you know the test results cannot support. Everyone else is nodding.
example.before: Stay quiet now and let the slip speak for itself later; or blurt out, in front of everyone, that the plan is fantasy.
example.after: Ask for two minutes, lay out the test data and what it implies for the date, frame it as protecting the launch the director cares about, and follow up privately afterwards.
example.why: Silence avoids risk at the cost of the goal, and a reckless outburst takes risk without judgment. The wiser response accepts a real personal cost for a worthy aim, and uses preparation, framing and follow-up so the risk actually serves that aim.

title: Death awareness
summary: The knowledge that one will die, and the ways that knowledge shapes how people think, feel and choose: it can prompt anxious defence of one's worldview and self-image, or a clearer sense of what matters and a turn towards growth, relationships and values.

title: Deliberation
summary: The capacity to think a choice through before acting: working out, for something that is up to you and whose outcome is uncertain, which available course will best reach a worthwhile end, and then settling on it.
selfCheck: Is this decision actually within my power, and is the outcome really uncertain, or am I deliberating to put off accepting something?
Have I checked that the goal itself is a good one, not just how to reach it?
Did I consider more than one way forward before settling on the first idea I had?
Is my confidence here earned by long, well-fed-back experience, or is it just a strong feeling?
Have I set a point where thinking stops and acting starts?
steps: Check that the matter is actually up to you and that its outcome is genuinely uncertain; if not, stop deliberating and either accept it or act on what is known.
Say plainly what you are trying to achieve, and ask whether that end is worth pursuing before you plan how to reach it.
List at least two or three realistic ways of getting there, not just the first one that occurred to you.
For the most promising option, trace backwards from the goal to the very next thing you would have to do, and drop options whose chain hits something impossible.
If the decision is important, talk it through with someone who knows this kind of situation.
Before trusting a strong gut feeling, ask whether you have had long, well-fed-back experience with situations like this one.
Set a point at which deliberation ends, then choose and act promptly, without reopening the question unless new facts appear.

example.situation: A manager has to decide within a week whether to move a struggling analyst to a different team or keep coaching her in her current role.
example.before: My gut says she's not cut out for this. I'll announce the move on Monday and be done with it.
example.after: Is this really my call, and what am I trying to achieve: her success, or a quieter team? Let me list the options, including a coaching plan with a review date, talk it over with HR and her previous lead, and decide by Thursday.
example.why: The wiser response clarifies the goal, widens the options and borrows others' judgment on an important, uncertain matter, but still commits to a decision on time instead of drifting.

title: Dichotomy of control
summary: The Stoic teaching, set out at the start of Epictetus's Handbook, that some things are up to us (our judgments, intentions, desires and choices) and others are not (body, property, reputation, outcomes), and that peace of mind and good action come from putting our care and effort where our agency actually lies.
selfCheck: Which part of this situation actually responds to what I decide or do next?
Am I treating something I could change as if it were fixed, just to avoid acting?
Am I staking my peace of mind on an outcome that other people or chance will settle?

example.situation: A team lead has submitted a strong proposal for next year's budget and now has to wait three weeks for a committee to decide, while rumours suggest cuts.
example.before: I keep refreshing my inbox and replaying what the committee might think. If they say no, the whole year was wasted.
example.after: The decision isn't mine. What is mine: answering their questions well, briefing my team honestly, and drafting a smaller fallback plan. I'll do those this week and stop checking for news.
example.why: Effort moves to the parts of the situation that respond to it, the outcome is still wanted and planned for, and the waiting no longer decides how the week goes.

title: Aristotle's doctrine of the mean
summary: Aristotle's teaching that each virtue of character is a settled disposition to feel and act at the intermediate point between a vice of excess and a vice of deficiency, where that point is fixed not by arithmetic but by what the situation and the person call for, as a practically wise person would judge.
selfCheck: Which way do I usually err in situations like this one, too much or too little, and am I correcting for it?
Am I calling a choice "balanced" just because it sits halfway between two options, rather than because it fits the situation?
Is the strength of my reaction proportionate to how serious this actually is?

example.situation: A newly promoted team lead has to tell a long-serving colleague that his reports keep arriving late and incomplete.
example.before: Either I let it slide to keep the peace, or I lay it all out bluntly in front of the team so nobody can say I'm soft.
example.after: I tend to avoid conflict, so I'll lean a little firmer than feels natural: a private conversation, the specific facts, what I need by when, and a real question about what is getting in his way.
example.why: The right degree of firmness depends on this person and this problem, and knowing which way you usually err tells you which way to correct, as Aristotle advised.

title: Emotional suppression
summary: Habitually hiding the outward signs of a feeling (face, voice, posture) once it is already under way, instead of changing how the situation is understood; it calms the surface without calming the feeling, and as a default habit it tends to cost memory, closeness and well-being.
selfCheck: Am I hiding this feeling because the moment calls for it, or because I always hide feelings like this?
Has the feeling actually changed, or only my face?
Is there someone I could tell how this really landed, and have I told them?
Could I look at the situation differently, rather than just clamping down on my reaction to it?

example.situation: In a project review, a senior colleague dismisses your team's proposal in front of everyone. You feel a hot rush of anger and embarrassment.
example.before: Keep a blank face, say 'fine', move on, and never mention it to anyone. Feelings have no place at work.
example.after: Stay composed in the room, since this isn't the moment, but name it briefly: 'I see it differently; can we go through the data after?' Later, ask what the criticism might be getting right, and talk it over with a trusted peer.
example.why: Holding back a display for a few minutes can fit the setting; making a rule of never showing or sharing the feeling leaves it running underneath, blurs what you take in, and keeps others from knowing where you stand.

title: Empathy
summary: The capacity to sense and share what another person feels, and to understand it from their point of view, while keeping clear that the feeling is theirs and not your own.
selfCheck: Have I actually tried to understand how this looks from their side, or am I assuming I already know?
Am I feeling with them, or am I now caught up in my own distress about their distress?
Is my empathy here going only to the person who is closest, most like me or most vivid, while others affected stay invisible?
After understanding what they feel, what would actually help them, as opposed to what would relieve my discomfort?

example.situation: A colleague tells you, close to tears, that their project has been cancelled after months of work, and you have your own deadline in an hour.
example.before: I absorb their upset so fully that I feel sick about it too, then I either pile on about how unfair management is or quietly avoid them for the rest of the week because it is too much.
example.after: I take a minute to really listen and say it back: 'Months of work, and it's gone. That's a real loss.' I notice the heaviness in me, remind myself it is their loss, not mine, and ask what would help. Later I check in and offer a concrete hand with the next project.
example.why: Feeling with someone opens the door, but staying clear about whose feeling it is and turning it into warm concern and practical help keeps you from either drowning in their distress or backing away from it.

title: Emulating moral exemplars
summary: Deliberately learning good judgment and character from people who already show it: noticing what a wiser person does in a particular situation, working out the reasons behind it, and turning the admiring pang of "I'm not there yet" into concrete attempts of your own, rather than into envy or hero-worship.
selfCheck: Whose judgment would I trust most in exactly this kind of situation, and what would they notice first?
Am I copying what my role model did, or what they were trying to achieve?
When I compare myself with someone better at this, am I working out my next step or looking for reasons to dismiss them?
Is the person I'm learning from close enough to my own circumstances that their example is one I can actually follow?
Are there flaws in my role model I've stopped being willing to see?
steps: Pick two or three people whose judgment you trust in a domain that matters to you now (a manager who handles conflict well, a relative who stays fair under pressure), and prefer people close to your own situation over distant heroes.
Watch for a specific moment where they acted well, and write down what they noticed, what they did and what they chose not to do.
Ask them, or work out, the reasons behind it, so that you learn the ideal the action served rather than only the gesture.
When you feel the sting of falling short, name the specific good you lack and one small step toward it this week, instead of looking for faults in them.
Try the step in a comparable situation of your own, adapted to your circumstances, then compare the result with what they did and why.
Widen and update your set of exemplars over time, and drop any you find yourself copying blindly or defending against all criticism.

example.situation: A newly promoted team lead has to tell a long-serving colleague that a project they championed is being cancelled. A senior manager in the next department is known for handling news like this well.
example.before: The new lead either copies the senior manager's breezy phrases word for word, or quietly decides that the manager is just naturally charismatic and that there's nothing to learn, and sends a short email.
example.after: The lead asks the manager how they handled a similar conversation, learns that they always explain the reason in person, acknowledge what the work achieved and offer the person a real role in what comes next, and plans a face-to-face meeting that does those three things in the lead's own words.
example.why: Emulation borrows the reasoning and the ideal behind an experienced person's choices, not their surface style, and it turns admiration into a concrete step the learner can actually take.

title: Epicureanism
summary: A Hellenistic school of philosophy founded by Epicurus in Athens around 306 BCE, which teaches that pleasure, understood as freedom from bodily pain and mental disturbance (ataraxia), is the goal of life, and that it is reached through prudence, limited desires, friendship and a clear understanding of nature, death and the gods.

title: Equanimity
summary: An even, balanced state of mind toward whatever happens, pleasant, painful or neutral: still feeling and still caring, but not being swept into craving, aversion or panic, so that you can see clearly and act well.
selfCheck: Am I reacting to what actually happened, or to the story I am telling about it?
Is my calm here steadiness, or am I simply refusing to feel or to care?
If this turned out well, or badly, would I still be able to act on my values?
What part of this is up to me, and am I putting my energy there?

example.situation: An hour before you present to leadership, you learn that the client your team spent three months courting has chosen a competitor.
example.before: This is a disaster. I'll open with who dropped the ball, and frankly I'm not sure this team can win anything.
example.after: That hurts, and I'll let myself feel it. What's in my hands now is an honest account of what we learned and what we'll try differently, so that's what I'll present.
example.why: The loss is still felt, but it no longer chooses your words; attention moves from blame and panic to the part of the situation you can actually shape.

title: Evening review
summary: A brief, regular look back at the day before sleep, asking what you did well, where you fell short of your own standards and what you will do differently tomorrow; taught in Pythagorean, Stoic and Confucian sources and aimed at steady improvement rather than self-punishment.
selfCheck: Am I reviewing today's conduct to improve it tomorrow, or to punish myself for it?
Have I named what went well today, and why, as well as where I fell short?
Is there one concrete thing I will say or do differently tomorrow as a result of this review?
Am I judging myself by my own considered standards, or by one bad moment?
steps: Pick a fixed, short slot at the end of the day, such as the last ten minutes before bed, and keep it whether or not the day went well.
Go through the day in order, recalling what you said and did in the main conversations, decisions and tasks, as if replaying it for a fair observer.
Ask three questions of each moment that stands out - what did I do well, where did I fall short of my own standards, and what did I leave undone?
For each shortfall, name the specific thing you would say or do next time, then let it go as Seneca did, with a pardon rather than a sentence.
Write down one good thing that happened and why it happened, so the review does not become a list of faults.
Choose a single intention for tomorrow and, every week or so, look back over your notes for patterns that keep recurring.

example.situation: During an afternoon planning meeting you cut off a junior colleague who was raising a scheduling concern, and later in the day the concern turned out to be right.
example.before: You lie awake replaying the moment, call yourself a terrible manager, check your phone to escape the feeling, and the next morning act as if nothing happened.
example.after: In a ten-minute review before bed you note that the meeting was otherwise well run, that you interrupted because you were defending a deadline you had promised, and that the concern was valid. You decide to thank the colleague tomorrow and to ask for objections before closing future planning meetings, then put the notebook away.
example.why: A fair, bounded review turns a sting into a specific repair and a better habit, whereas unstructured replay punishes you without changing what happens next.

title: Folly
summary: The practical opposite of wisdom: acting with more confidence than one's knowledge, self-knowledge or self-control warrants, and ignoring others' interests and long-term consequences. Psychologists stress that folly is not the same as low intelligence; bright, successful people are often especially prone to it.
selfCheck: Do I actually have the specific knowledge or skill this action needs, or am I borrowing confidence from success somewhere else?
Whose interests, besides mine, does this decision affect, and how will it look in a year rather than this week?
Am I assuming the consequences won't reach me because of my position, record or cleverness?
When someone questioned this plan, did I answer their point or just wave it away?

example.situation: A senior engineer, the most experienced person on the team, wants to push a database change to the live system late on a Friday. A junior colleague asks whether it has been tested against a copy of the real data.
example.before: "I've done this kind of change a hundred times. Testing it would take all afternoon, and nothing is going to break." The change goes out unreviewed, fails over the weekend, and the on-call staff spend two days repairing it.
example.after: "Fair question. My experience is with the old schema, not this one, so I don't actually know. Let's run it against the staging copy and ship on Monday, when people are around if it goes wrong." The test exposes a locking problem, which is fixed before release.
example.why: Expertise in one area tempts people to feel knowledgeable and safe everywhere; asking what this particular action requires, who bears the cost if it fails, and whether a dissenting question has been answered brings confidence back into line with what is actually known.

title: Forgiveness
summary: The settled readiness to give up resentment and the wish for revenge toward someone who wronged you, while still judging that what they did was wrong, without requiring that you forget, excuse or reconcile.
selfCheck: Am I holding on to this to protect myself or someone else, or mainly to make them pay?
Have I separated forgiving from excusing, forgetting and reconciling, so I know which of these I'm actually being asked to do?
If they keep doing this, what boundary would self-respect require alongside any forgiveness?
Have I given myself time to name the hurt before deciding whether, and how, to forgive?

example.situation: A colleague presented your analysis as their own to a client, later admitted it and apologised, and you still have to work together on the account.
example.before: I'll be polite, but I'm keeping score, and I'll make sure the client finds out what they're really like.
example.after: I'll tell them plainly that it was wrong and that I'll put my name on my own work from now on. Then I'll stop rehearsing it and treat them fairly on this project.
example.why: Forgiving here means dropping the campaign of payback while keeping the judgement that it was wrong and the safeguards that protect you; it is neither pretending nothing happened nor trusting blindly.

title: The four immeasurables
summary: A Buddhist framework of four boundless attitudes toward all beings, loving-kindness (mettā), compassion (karuṇā), sympathetic joy (muditā) and equanimity (upekkhā), cultivated together so that each one corrects the typical failure of the others.
selfCheck: Can I be glad about this person's success, or am I quietly keeping score?
Is what I am calling compassion here help for them, or my own distress at their pain?
Is my calm the steadiness of seeing clearly, or have I simply stopped caring?
Would I offer this same goodwill to someone I find difficult, or only to people on my side?
steps: Name the situation in front of you: someone is doing well, someone is suffering, someone is simply there, or the outcome is out of your hands.
Choose the quality that fits it, goodwill for the ordinary encounter, compassion for suffering, sympathetic joy for another's success and equanimity for what you cannot change.
Check the quality for its look-alike, asking whether goodwill has become clinging, compassion has become your own distress, joy has become excitement or calm has become not caring.
Widen the circle one step, offering the same attitude to someone neutral or difficult, not only to people you already like.
Afterwards, notice which of the four came easily and which you avoided, and practise the neglected one next time.

example.situation: A peer you trained wins the promotion you also applied for, on the same day another teammate tells you their project has just been cancelled.
example.before: I congratulate the winner through gritted teeth, then spend lunch with the other teammate agreeing that management is hopeless, and leave work feeling worse about both of them.
example.after: I let the disappointment register, then congratulate my peer properly and mean it. With the teammate I listen and ask what would help, without stoking the grievance, and I accept that the promotion decision is made and no longer mine to change.
example.why: Each person needed a different response; sympathetic joy keeps envy from souring the success, compassion meets the setback, and equanimity stops your own loss from colouring both.

title: Giving advice
summary: The situation of being asked, or feeling moved, to tell someone else what they should do about a problem in their life or work — a test of wisdom that psychologists have used to measure it, and one where good intentions often go wrong.
selfCheck: Did the person actually ask for my advice, or am I volunteering it?
Do I understand their situation and constraints, or am I answering the problem I once had?
Have I explained my reasoning, so they can judge it rather than just obey it?
Am I giving this advice for their sake, or because being the one who knows feels good?
If they decide differently, can I let it go?

example.situation: A colleague stops by your desk and says she has been offered a promotion to manage her current team, but isn't sure she wants it. You once took a similar step and loved it.
example.before: Take it. I did exactly the same thing and it was the best move I ever made. You'll regret it forever if you say no.
example.after: Congratulations. Before I say what I think, what's making you hesitate? … It sounds as if the worry is managing two close friends. I'm not you, so take this as one view: when I faced that, what helped was talking to them early. Who else knows this team well that you could ask?
example.why: The wiser response listens first, finds out what the real question is, offers a view as one perspective with its reasoning shown, and leaves the decision with the person who has to live with it.

title: Golden Rule
summary: The widely shared moral maxim to treat others as you would want to be treated, in a positive form ("do to others what you would have them do to you") or a negative one ("do not do to others what you would not want done to you"); best read as a habit of imaginative fairness, checked against what the other person actually wants.
selfCheck: If our positions were reversed, would I accept being treated the way I'm about to treat this person?
Am I applying my own tastes, or the underlying respect I'd want, and have I asked what they actually want?
Would I be comfortable if everyone in my position acted on the reason I'm acting on now?
Does this relationship's difference in power change what treating them as an equal would require?

example.situation: A manager wants to thank a quiet, highly reliable analyst for rescuing a delayed project.
example.before: I'd love to be praised in front of the whole department, so I'll call her up at the all-hands and give a big speech.
example.after: What I'd want is to have my effort noticed and valued. I'll ask her how she likes to be recognised; she prefers a note to her director and first pick of the next project, so that is what she gets.
example.why: The manager keeps the rule's core (give the respect and appreciation you'd want) but stops projecting a personal taste onto someone who doesn't share it, which is the most common way the rule misfires.

title: Gratitude
summary: The settled disposition to recognise goods you have received, to see that they came from the goodwill of someone else, and to respond with fitting thanks and goodwill in return, without servility or a ledger of debts.
selfCheck: Have I noticed who made this good thing possible, and the effort or intention it took them?
Have I actually told them, specifically, rather than only feeling it?
Is my thanks free, or am I acting out of a sense of debt, guilt or deference I don't really owe?
Am I using "be grateful" to talk myself, or someone else, out of a legitimate complaint?

example.situation: A teammate quietly stayed late to fix a broken data feed so your quarterly report could go out on time.
example.before: Good, it's fixed. That's their job anyway; on to the next thing.
example.after: I'll tell them specifically what their evening saved, mention it to our manager, and keep an eye out for a chance to help them in turn.
example.why: Gratitude notices both the benefit and the goodwill behind it, then answers with thanks and goodwill rather than taking it for granted or treating it as a debt to settle and forget.

title: Grief and bereavement
summary: The situation of having lost someone close through death, and the grief that follows: a mix of yearning, sorrow, disbelief and gradual acceptance that unfolds differently for each person rather than in fixed stages. Wisdom here means making room for both remembering and rebuilding, and knowing when grief needs more help.
selfCheck: Am I judging my grief, or someone else's, against a schedule of stages that the evidence does not support?
Have I made room both for remembering the person and for the practical and social life I still have to live?
Has intense yearning or numbness kept me from functioning most days for many months, so that it is time to talk to a professional?

example.situation: Two months after her father's death, Dana enjoys a weekend away with friends, then feels guilty and wonders whether she is grieving "wrong" because she has not hit a depression stage.
example.before: I'm supposed to be in the sad stage by now. If I can laugh, maybe I didn't love him enough, so I'll cancel the next plan.
example.after: Grief doesn't run on a timetable. Missing him and getting on with life can both be part of it, so I'll keep the plan and also set aside Sunday evening to look through his letters.
example.why: Research finds no fixed sequence of stages, and moving back and forth between facing the loss and rebuilding daily life is a normal, healthy pattern rather than a sign of loving less.

title: Hebrew wisdom literature
summary: The wisdom tradition of ancient Israel preserved in the Hebrew Bible, above all in Proverbs, Job and Ecclesiastes (with later books such as Ben Sira and the Wisdom of Solomon). Proverbs teaches practical skill in living well, while Job and Ecclesiastes test that teaching against undeserved suffering, chance and the limits of human understanding.

title: Hedonic and eudaimonic well-being
summary: The widely used framework in well-being research that separates hedonic well-being (pleasure, positive mood and life satisfaction) from eudaimonic well-being (meaning, growth, excellence and living by one's values); useful for reflecting on how one lives, but contested as a scientific division because self-report measures of the two overlap almost completely.
selfCheck: Am I treating enjoyment as frivolous, or meaning as a duty, rather than letting each do its own work in my life?
When I judge whether a choice will make me better off, am I thinking only about how it will feel this week, or also about whether it fits what I value and want to grow into?
Am I relying on a neat label (pleasure versus meaning) where my actual experience is more mixed?

example.situation: After a draining quarter, a team lead plans a free weekend and wonders how to spend it to feel restored.
example.before: Pleasure is shallow; I'll spend the weekend on a self-improvement course so the time counts for something.
example.after: I'll do one thing purely for enjoyment, like a long lunch with friends, and one thing I care about, like finishing the bookshelf I'm building with my kid, and see how each leaves me feeling on Monday and a month from now.
example.why: Research suggests pleasure-seeking and meaning-seeking pay off on different timescales and work best together, so treating one as the "real" happiness tends to shortchange the other.

title: Honesty
summary: The character trait of reliably not distorting the facts as you understand them, whether by lying, misleading, cheating, stealing or breaking promises, out of care for truth and for the people who depend on it rather than out of fear of being caught; practised wisely, it is joined to tact, timing and kindness rather than to bluntness.
selfCheck: If the other person later learned everything I know, would they feel I had misled them, even if every word I said was true?
Am I keeping quiet here out of tact, or out of fear of an awkward moment?
Is the kind thing I am about to say also accurate, and is the accurate thing I am about to say also kind?
What am I telling myself about my own part in this that I would not want someone else to check?

example.situation: Your manager asks, in front of the team, whether the migration you lead is on track for Friday. It is not; a data problem surfaced yesterday and you have not yet told anyone.
example.before: We're in good shape. There are a few loose ends, but nothing to worry about.
example.after: Not for Friday, as things stand. We found a data issue yesterday. I'll have a revised date and options to you by this afternoon.
example.why: The first answer contains no outright lie but is built to mislead, and it spends trust the team will need when the slip comes out. The second states the fact plainly, owns the delay, and pairs bad news with a next step.

title: Hubris
summary: An inflated, success-fed self-confidence that leads a person with power to overrate their own judgment, brush aside advice and criticism, and take overambitious risks; in ancient Greek the word named something narrower, the deliberate humiliation of others for the pleasure of feeling superior.
selfCheck: Am I dismissing this objection because of its evidence, or because of who raised it and how well things have gone for me lately?
When did someone last change my mind on something important, and did I make it easy or costly for them?
Who, if anyone, can still stop me from making this decision, and have I given them what they need to do so?
Am I treating my organisation's success as proof of my own judgment?

example.situation: A department head has delivered three strong years in a row and been praised in the trade press. A senior analyst warns that a proposed expansion rests on optimistic demand figures.
example.before: "I've called it right every time so far, and the numbers will catch up with the vision. We're not slowing down for a spreadsheet." The analyst stops raising concerns, and the plan goes ahead unchanged.
example.after: "My recent wins are a reason to check myself, not to skip the check. Walk me through your demand figures, and let's have finance stress-test both versions before the board sees either." The plan is approved a quarter later at a smaller scale, with a review point.
example.why: Recent success and praise are exactly the conditions under which leaders overpay and overreach; deliberately inviting the dissenting case and an independent check restores the feedback that power tends to cut off.

title: Humble leadership
aliases: leading by modelling how to grow
summary: A way of leading in which the person in charge openly admits their own limits and mistakes, gives visible credit for others' strengths and contributions, and shows they are still learning, so that the team treats growth and honest uncertainty as normal.
selfCheck: When did I last tell my team, in so many words, that I was wrong about something?
Who did the real work on this result, and have the people above me heard their names?
Am I asking for input because I will use it, or to look open?
Does this situation call for listening and learning, or for a fast, clear decision that I can review with the team later?
steps: When you get something wrong or don't know the answer, say so plainly and early, and say what you will do about it.
Name specific contributions by specific people, in their hearing and when reporting upward; say "we" for shared wins and "I" for your own errors.
Ask the team for feedback on one concrete thing you did, listen without defending, and tell them later what you changed.
Let people with more expertise on a task teach you, in front of others if possible.
Keep making clear decisions; in a crisis or under tight deadlines, act first and invite reflection afterwards.
Check that the humility is believed, not read as a tactic, by keeping your private conduct consistent with what you say in meetings.

example.situation: A project lead's schedule for a product launch slips by three weeks, partly because she under-estimated the testing work, and an analyst on the team had flagged the risk early.
example.before: The vendors let us down and testing turned out harder than anyone could have predicted. We'll push harder.
example.after: I under-estimated testing, and Priya flagged it in March; I should have listened. Here's the revised plan. Priya, can you walk me through how you sized it so I get it right next time?
example.why: Owning the error, crediting the person who saw it and asking to learn from her makes it safe for others to raise risks early, and it fixes the estimating method rather than just the date.

title: Igor Grossmann
summary: Social and cultural psychologist at the University of Waterloo, director of its Wisdom and Culture Lab, whose studies of how people reason about conflicts showed that wise reasoning can be measured, varies with age, culture and situation, and is weaker about one's own problems than about other people's.

title: Ikigai
summary: An everyday Japanese word for what makes life feel worth living, and for the felt sense of having it; research treats it as close to eudaimonic well-being. The popular Western "ikigai" Venn diagram of passion, skill, need and pay is a recent business-coaching overlay, not the Japanese concept, and claims that ikigai lengthens life outrun the observational evidence.

title: Imaginary future generations
summary: A deliberation practice from the Future Design movement in which some members of a group are asked to imagine themselves living decades ahead and to argue and negotiate on behalf of those future people, so that a decision made today gives voice to those who will inherit its consequences but cannot take part in it.
selfCheck: Who will live with this decision after I have moved on, and has anyone in the room spoken for them?
If I were a member of that future group, what would I ask today's decision-makers to protect?
Am I treating my guess about future people's wishes as a certainty, or as one voice to weigh?
Have I written down my reasons so that my successors can see and judge them?
steps: Name the decision and choose a horizon year far enough ahead (often 25–40 years) that most people in the room will no longer be in charge.
Ask one person, or a separate group, to imagine they actually live in that year and to speak as its residents, staff or customers, rather than simply forecasting.
Have the future side describe what the place is like and what they wish today's decision-makers had done, then list their priorities from that standpoint.
Have the present side list its priorities from today's needs, without trying to anticipate the future group.
Bring both sides together to negotiate one shared plan, and record where the future side changed it and where it was overruled and why.
Rotate the role in later sessions so that everyone has spoken for the future at least once, and end by writing down reasons and advice for your successors.

example.situation: A department head is drafting next year's budget and is tempted to cut the apprenticeship programme, whose payoff arrives only after the current team has moved on.
example.before: Cut it. Nobody in this meeting will be here when those apprentices are senior, and we need the money for this year's targets.
example.after: Before deciding, ask two colleagues to speak as the department's staff in 2045: what will they need from us, and what would they say about this cut? Then weigh their case against this year's pressures, and write down why we chose what we chose.
example.why: The first response counts only the people present. The second gives the people who will inherit the decision a voice in the room and leaves a record they can judge us by, without pretending that their interests automatically win.

title: Impermanence
summary: The Buddhist teaching that every conditioned thing, including the body, feelings, thoughts and the sense of self, arises, changes and passes away, so that clinging to anything as fixed leads to suffering; versions of the insight also appear in Stoicism and in Heraclitus's philosophy of flux.
selfCheck: Am I treating something that is already changing as if it should stay exactly as it is?
If this difficult situation is temporary, how would I act differently today?
Is this good thing worth savouring more because it will not last?
Am I using "nothing lasts" to avoid caring or committing, rather than to see clearly?

example.situation: A project manager's team is reorganised; her favourite colleague moves to another group and the weekly rhythm she relied on disappears.
example.before: This was the best team I've ever had and they've wrecked it. I'll keep doing things the old way and wait for it to be put back.
example.after: That team was always going to change; people move on, and so will this new setup. I'll thank my old colleague properly, stay in touch, and figure out what this new group needs from me now.
example.why: The wiser response grieves what was good without demanding that it stay fixed, and puts energy into the situation as it actually is.

title: Implementation intentions
summary: Turning a decision you have already made into a specific if-then plan that names the situation in which you will act and exactly what you will do ("If it is 9 a.m. at my desk, then I open the report before the inbox"), so that the moment itself, rather than fresh willpower, triggers the better choice.
selfCheck: Have I named the exact moment when I will act, or only the goal I hope to reach?
What is the cue that usually pulls me off course, and do I have a then-response ready for it?
Do I still endorse this goal, or am I making plans to avoid admitting I no longer want it?
If I am about to drop the plan, has something genuinely changed, or has the moment of keeping it simply arrived?
steps: Check that the goal is one you have actually decided on and still endorse; if you are lukewarm about it, deliberate first, because a plan cannot supply commitment you do not have.
Identify the critical moment, either the opportunity to act (a time, a place, a recurring event) or the obstacle that usually derails you (a temptation, a distraction, a feeling).
Write one plan per cue in the form "If [specific situation], then I will [specific action]", making the cue concrete enough that you will recognise it and the action small enough to start at once.
For your usual obstacle, add a shielding plan, such as "If I feel the urge to check messages, then I will note it and keep writing until the timer ends."
Say or rehearse the plan a few times so the cue and the response are firmly linked, and remove anything in the setting that competes with it.
Afterwards, review whether the cue appeared and the plan fired; revise the plan if circumstances have genuinely changed, not merely because keeping it felt hard.

example.situation: A team lead has decided, for good reasons, to stop interrupting colleagues in meetings, but keeps doing it when a discussion gets heated.
example.before: "I'll just try harder to listen next week." In the next tense meeting the resolution is forgotten within minutes, and she cuts in twice.
example.after: "If I notice I'm about to speak while someone else is mid-sentence, then I'll write my point down and wait for them to finish." In the meeting, the urge to cut in becomes her cue to reach for the notepad.
example.why: A general resolution relies on remembering and summoning willpower at exactly the moment emotion is highest. An if-then plan decides in calm advance what the trigger is and what to do, so the situation itself prompts the wiser response.

title: Implicit theories of wisdom
summary: The ideas about what wisdom is, who is wise and how wisdom grows that ordinary people carry around, usually without having spelled them out; psychologists study them by asking laypeople to describe, rate or nominate wise people, and contrast them with the explicit theories built by researchers.
selfCheck: When I call someone wise, am I responding to their judgment and care for others, or mainly to their intelligence, confidence or age?
Whose advice am I about to rely on here, and what picture of wisdom made me choose them?
Would someone raised with a different idea of wisdom see this choice as wise, and what would they weigh that I am leaving out?

title: Intellectual humility
summary: The character trait of noticing and owning the limits of what you know and of how well you reason: admitting gaps and possible error to yourself and others, without either inflating your intellectual strengths or collapsing into self-doubt, because you care more about getting things right than about looking right.
selfCheck: Which part of my view have I actually checked, and which part am I only sure of?
What evidence or argument would change my mind here, and have I gone looking for it?
When I was shown a mistake just now, did I feel curiosity or did I feel attacked?
Am I underselling a strength I really do have, out of false modesty or fear of conflict?

example.situation: In a project review, a colleague points out that the sales forecast you built last month rests on an assumption you never checked.
example.before: The model is fine. The market just shifted; nobody could have seen that coming.
example.after: You're right, I didn't test that assumption. Let's rerun it with your figure and see how much the forecast moves. Thanks for catching it.
example.why: Owning the gap, rather than blaming circumstances or brushing it off, fixes the forecast, shows the team that errors can be raised safely, and treats the critic as an ally in getting it right.

title: Intellectual virtues
summary: Excellences of the mind: the states and traits that make someone good at grasping truth and thinking well. Aristotle named five (craft, scientific knowledge, practical wisdom, intuitive reason and theoretical wisdom); modern virtue epistemology adds character traits of a good inquirer such as curiosity, open-mindedness, intellectual humility, intellectual courage, carefulness and tenacity.
selfCheck: Before I settled on this view, did I actually look for the strongest case against it?
Am I being careful and thorough here, or just quick and confident?
Is my curiosity about this question real, or do I mainly want to be proved right?
Whose knowledge or testimony am I discounting, and is that because of the evidence or because of who they are?

title: Interpersonal conflict
summary: A clash of wants, views or expectations between people who matter to each other — partners, family, friends, colleagues — and one of the life situations where wise reasoning is most studied and most needed.
selfCheck: Am I sure I know why the other person acted as they did, or am I filling the gap with the least charitable story?
How would a neutral friend who wanted the best for both of us describe this argument?
How am I likely to see this disagreement a year from now?
Is there an outcome that meets the main concern on each side, or am I only trying to win?

example.situation: Two siblings are arguing about who should take on more of the care for an ageing parent. One lives nearby; the other earns more and lives two hours away. The latest phone call ended with both hanging up angry.
example.before: I'm the one doing everything while you just send money. You clearly don't care, and I'm done asking.
example.after: I'm exhausted and I said it badly. I don't actually know what this has been like for you from a distance. Can we each list what we can realistically give over the next six months and see what a fair split looks like? This arrangement doesn't have to be permanent.
example.why: The wiser response owns its part, admits what it doesn't know about the other person's position, allows that things can change, and looks for an arrangement both can live with instead of a verdict on who is the better child.

title: James J. Gross
summary: Stanford psychologist who did more than anyone to turn emotion regulation into a research field: his process model sorts the ways people shape their feelings by when they act, and his work with Oliver John made reappraisal and expressive suppression the two best-studied strategies; later researchers have questioned how far one strategy can be called good and the other bad.

title: Kill criteria
summary: Deciding at the outset of a goal or project which observable signals, checked by which dates, will mean you stop or seriously reconsider, so that the later decision to quit rests on evidence set out in advance rather than on what has already been spent.
selfCheck: Before I started, did I write down what result, by what date, would tell me to stop?
Is each criterion concrete enough that someone else could tell whether it has been met?
Now that a criterion has been tripped, is my reason for carrying on new information, or what I have already put in?
Am I counting my time and effort against the budget, not only the money?
Who without a stake in the original decision could check this call?
steps: When you commit to a goal or project, write down two to four signals that would show it is failing, each paired with a date by which you will check it.
Make each signal concrete and, where you can, numeric, such as a minimum level of sales, sign-ups, savings or progress, so that someone else could tell whether it has been met.
Set a budget for the effort as well as the money, counting hours, weekends and favours, because time spent tends to escape the books.
Share the criteria with someone who had no stake in starting the project and ask them to hold you to them, or to make the stop-or-go call themselves.
On each review date, compare results with the criteria and ask whether, starting from scratch today, you would begin this.
When a criterion is tripped, treat stopping as the default; continue only if you can write down new information that justifies it, not the cost already sunk.
When you stop, record what you learned, give credit for the progress made, and name the next goal the freed time and money will go to.

example.situation: A café owner started a weekday lunch-delivery service three months ago, buying a used van and training two drivers. Orders are well below what she hoped and the service loses money every week.
example.before: We've bought the van and trained the drivers, so stopping now would waste all that. Let's push on until the summer and see if word of mouth picks up.
example.after: When we launched I wrote that we'd stop if we weren't at forty orders a day by the end of month three. We're at eighteen. I'll end deliveries next week, sell the van, and put the two most-ordered dishes on the counter menu.
example.why: The first response weighs what has been spent; the second applies a test set before any results came in, when judgment was not yet coloured by investment and pride, and pairs the exit with a next step.

title: Know thyself
summary: The ancient Greek maxim inscribed at Apollo's temple at Delphi, read first as a reminder of human limits and later, through Socrates and Plato, as a call to examine one's own character, beliefs and ignorance; modern psychology adds that this is best done with the help of other people's views.
selfCheck: What would someone who knows me well say about me here that I would rather not hear?
Am I judging myself by my intentions while others can only see my behaviour?
Have I mistaken a confident story about my motives for real knowledge of them?

example.situation: After a project review, a manager is told by two team members that her meetings run long because she rarely lets others finish a point.
example.before: That's not me. I know how I come across, and I'm a good listener.
example.after: I don't experience myself that way, but two people saw the same thing. I'll ask a colleague to watch the next meeting and tell me what they notice.
example.why: Self-views are least reliable on flattering or unflattering traits, so treating others' observations as evidence rather than an attack is how the maxim is actually followed.

title: Knowing when to quit
summary: The capacity to tell a goal worth persisting with from one that has become unattainable or too costly, to withdraw effort and commitment from the second kind, and to redirect that energy into new goals worth pursuing.
selfCheck: If I were deciding today from scratch, with no time or money already spent, would I choose to start this?
Am I persisting because the goal is still reachable and worth it, or because quitting would mean admitting I was wrong?
What new goal will this time and energy go to if I let this one go?
Am I giving up because this is unattainable, or only because the current stretch is hard?

example.situation: A team lead has spent eighteen months on an internal software tool that users keep ignoring; a cheaper commercial product now does the same job, and the next budget review is in a month.
example.before: We've put too much into this to stop now. One more release and people will come round, so I'll ask for another two developers.
example.after: If we were starting today, would we fund this? No. I'll show the review the adoption numbers and the alternative, propose winding it down by the quarter's end, and move the team onto the reporting backlog everyone keeps asking for.
example.why: The wiser response judges the project on what it will deliver from here rather than on what it has already cost, which is the pull behind escalation, and it pairs stopping with a clear next goal, which is where the well-being benefits of letting go appear.

title: Leading others
summary: The situation of being responsible for other people's work and growth — as a manager, team lead, coach or project head — where your decisions affect people who have less say than you, and where the power you hold can quietly change how well you listen and judge.
selfCheck: Am I weighing my colleagues' advice as seriously as I would have before I had authority over them?
When nobody objected in that meeting, did I check whether they agreed or just stayed quiet?
Whose interests does this decision touch beyond the targets I am measured on?
Am I still doing the work myself because it is needed, or because it is where I feel competent?

example.situation: A newly promoted team lead, formerly the team's strongest engineer, sees a colleague's design for a new service and is sure her own approach would be faster to build.
example.before: I'm the lead now, so we'll do it my way. I'll rewrite the plan tonight and hand out the tasks tomorrow.
example.after: Ask the colleague to walk the team through the design and its trade-offs, put the alternative on the table as one option rather than an order, ask who sees risks in either, and agree how the choice will be made and reviewed.
example.why: Relying on title wins compliance at best and silences the people closest to the work; inviting their view and weighing it treats authority as responsibility for the decision rather than a licence to skip other people's knowledge.

title: Learning from experience
summary: The ordinary but demanding situation of trying to turn what has happened to you, good or bad, into better judgment next time. Wisdom here means connecting what you did with what followed, examining successes as well as failures, and exploring an experience for what it can teach rather than merely living through it or tying it up in a comforting story.
selfCheck: Can I say what I did, what followed, and how I think the two are connected?
Am I examining this to understand it, or only to feel better about it and close the chapter?
Have I looked at what went well and why, not only at what went wrong?
Whose view of this experience would challenge my own version of it?

example.situation: In the space of a year, three people on a small team you manage have resigned, each giving a different reason on the way out.
example.before: You decide it was bad luck and a hot job market, tell yourself the team is stronger for the turnover, and move straight on to hiring replacements.
example.after: You lay the three departures side by side, note what you did in the months before each one and what followed, ask one former colleague who left on good terms what they saw, and notice that all three had asked for a change of scope that you postponed. You commit to discussing growth plans with every remaining report this quarter.
example.why: The first response is a redemptive story that brings closure but no lesson; the second connects your own actions with their consequences and explores the pattern, which is the kind of processing linked to wisdom.

title: Linda A. Hill
summary: Harvard Business School professor whose year-long study of first-time managers, published as Becoming a Manager (1992), made the move into leading others a subject of research: she showed it to be a slow change of identity learned through experience, in which authority rests on earned credibility rather than on the title.

title: Logotherapy
