summary: Viktor Frankl's meaning-centred approach to psychotherapy and to life, which holds that the search for meaning is a basic human motive and that meaning can be found through what we create, what and whom we experience, and the attitude we take toward suffering we cannot avoid.
selfCheck: Am I asking what I want from life, or what this situation is asking of me?
Is there anything left for me to create, experience or stand for here, even if the outcome is out of my hands?
Am I watching myself so closely that it is getting in the way of what I'm trying to do?
steps: Name one thing you are creating or contributing right now, however small, and who it serves.
Name one experience or person you value that you could give more attention to this week.
For a hardship you cannot change, decide what stance toward it you want to be able to look back on.
Turn your attention from monitoring yourself to the task or person in front of you.

example.situation: A team's long-running project is cancelled after a reorganisation, and a project lead feels the past year was wasted.
example.before: None of it mattered. I'll keep my head down and stop caring about the work.
example.after: The project is gone, but the people I trained and what we learned stay. What do I want to build next, and how do I want to carry this?
example.why: Looking for meaning in contribution, relationships and chosen attitude, rather than only in outcomes you control, keeps a setback from emptying out the whole effort.

title: Major life decisions
summary: The rare, high-stakes choices that reshape a life — whether to change career, move, start or end a relationship, or have a child — where the outcome is uncertain, hard to undo, and may change the very person who lives with it.
selfCheck: Am I treating "not deciding" as if it were not itself a choice?
Am I assuming the person I'll be in ten years wants exactly what I want today?
Which part of this can I learn about before committing, and which part can I only learn by living it?

example.situation: After eight years in a stable accounting job, Priya has an offer to retrain as a teacher at lower pay, and has been going back and forth for months.
example.before: I'll wait until I'm sure I'll be happier as a teacher. Until then, staying put is the safe choice.
example.after: I can't know now what teaching will feel like, and staying is a choice too. I'll test what I can (shadow a class, ask two teachers what surprised them), decide what I'd want to have tried, and set a date.
example.why: Waiting for a certainty that can't arrive quietly chooses the status quo, which the evidence suggests people over-favour; gathering what is knowable and naming the real reasons is the wiser path.

title: Meaning in life
summary: The sense that one's life makes sense, has direction and matters: in psychology, a judgment with three facets (coherence, purpose and significance); in philosophy, the question of what, beyond happiness and morality, makes an individual life worthwhile.
selfCheck: Is what feels missing right now coherence, direction, or a sense that this is worth doing?
Am I treating a bad week or a low mood as a verdict on my whole life?
Would I still judge this pursuit worthwhile if I stopped feeling drawn to it, and would I still care about it if no one else valued it?

example.situation: After a reorganisation, an analyst's work is folded into another team and she starts to feel that her job, and her weeks, no longer add up to anything.
example.before: None of this matters, so I'll stop caring, coast, and wait until I feel inspired to find my calling.
example.after: Which part is missing: does the work no longer make sense to me, have I lost direction, or do I doubt it is worth doing? Let me fix the piece I can, starting with who actually relies on what I do.
example.why: Splitting meaning into coherence, purpose and significance turns a vague sense of emptiness into a specific, workable question, and meaning tends to follow connection and contribution rather than waiting for a revelation.

title: Memento mori
summary: The deliberate, regular practice of remembering that you will die and do not know when, used not to dwell on death but to see more clearly what deserves your time, attention and care today.
selfCheck: If my time were shorter than I assume, would this still be worth my anger or effort?
Am I using the thought of death to clarify what matters, or to feed dread or reckless indulgence?
What would I want to have said or done for the people involved here?
steps: Pick a fixed cue for the reflection, such as waking up, a commute, or the last few minutes before sleep.
Bring to mind, concretely and in your own case, that your life will end and that you do not know when.
Look back over the last day or week and ask how you actually spent your time and attention.
Ask what you would regret leaving undone or unsaid, and whom you would think of first.
Choose one concrete action for today that reflects what matters, and let go of one petty grievance or craving.
Return your attention to the task in front of you; if the reflection leaves you more anxious than clear, shorten it or stop.

example.situation: You have spent a week stewing over a curt email from a colleague and are drafting a sharp reply late in the evening while your family is in the next room.
example.before: I'll send a reply that puts them in their place, then keep going through my inbox until midnight.
example.after: If my time were shorter than I assume, this exchange would not be worth another evening. I'll send a short, civil reply tomorrow and spend tonight with the people in the next room.
example.why: Remembering that time is limited and uncertain shifts attention from winning a minor status contest to the relationships and values you would actually want to have served.

title: Mono no aware
aliases: sensitivity to the transience of things
summary: A classical Japanese ideal of feeling deeply moved by things because they pass: an empathetic, often bittersweet sensitivity to the fleeting beauty of nature and human life, which the scholar Motoori Norinaga made the central concept of Japanese literature.

title: Moral algebra
summary: Benjamin Franklin's method for a hard choice: list the reasons for and against in two columns over several days, give each a rough weight, strike out reasons of equal weight on opposite sides, and decide by where the balance lies.
selfCheck: Did I collect reasons over a few days, or only those that occurred to me in one mood?
Did I weigh the reasons, or just count which column was longer?
Is there one reason so important that it should settle this on its own, whatever the rest of the list says?
Am I using the list to choose, or to talk myself out of something I had already decided to do?
Now that the balance is clear, have I set a time to act on it?
steps: Use the method only for an important choice that is up to you and genuinely two-sided, not for a matter of taste or a change you have already committed to.
Frame one specific option (for example, "accept the transfer") and divide a page into two columns headed Pro and Con.
Over three or four days, add a short note to either column whenever a reason occurs to you, instead of trying to list everything in one sitting.
Bring all the reasons into view and give each a rough weight, such as 1 to 3.
Strike out pairs of reasons of equal weight on opposite sides, and let one strong reason cancel two or three weaker ones that together equal it.
Ask whether any single remaining reason is decisive on its own, or whether a reason you never wrote down is the one actually driving you.
Wait a day or two; if no important new reason appears, decide by the balance and act on it.

example.situation: A project manager is offered a two-year posting to the company's office in another city and has to reply within a week.
example.before: It sounds exciting and I hate saying no to leadership. I'll accept in tomorrow's one-to-one and sort out the details later.
example.after: I'll keep a Pro and Con page on my phone for the next four days, weigh the reasons on Friday, and see what's left after cancelling the equal ones. If the only big thing on the Con side is my partner's job, that's a conversation to have before I answer, not a line to cancel out.
example.why: Gathering reasons over several days stops the mood of one meeting from deciding, weighing rather than counting keeps a single heavy reason from being outvoted by trivia, and the final check surfaces the reason that really matters.

title: Moral case deliberation
summary: A facilitated group dialogue in which professionals take a morally difficult case from their own work, state the dilemma, weigh the values of everyone involved and each say what they would do and why, so as to understand the case better, act more wisely in it and build the team's practical judgment.
selfCheck: Can I state the dilemma as two concrete options, and say what harm each would do and to whom?
Have I understood the case from the position of the person who has to act, before judging it?
Whose values and perspective are missing from how we have framed this case?
Am I trying to understand my colleagues' reasons, or only to win them over to my view?
Who will act on what we concluded, and when will we look again at how it went?
steps: Choose a real, current case from your own work that leaves you or your team unsure what is right, and ask someone trained and not involved in the decision to facilitate.
State the moral question as a concrete choice between two options, and name the harm each option would do.
Ask factual questions until everyone can stand in the case presenter's shoes, without judging how they handled it.
List everyone with a stake in the case and the values and norms that pull each of them towards one option or the other.
Look for alternatives beyond the original two options.
Each write down privately what you would do, the value behind it, what you would sacrifice, how you would limit that damage and what you would need to act on it.
Compare the answers in dialogue, exploring the reasons behind disagreements rather than voting or trying to win.
Close by asking what has changed in each person's view, who will act on what, and what to improve in the next session.

example.situation: A home-care team disagrees about an elderly client who refuses help with washing. Some nurses want to insist for hygiene and dignity; others say his refusal must be respected. Tension is growing and each shift handles it differently.
example.before: The team lead sends an email setting a rule, help with washing twice a week whether he likes it or not, and treats further objections as insubordination.
example.after: The team lead books an hour with a trained facilitator. The nurse closest to the client presents the case, the team names what is at stake on each side (his autonomy, his health, the relationship, staff integrity), finds an option nobody had considered, and agrees a shared approach to try and review in a month.
example.why: The rule settles the behaviour but not the moral question, so the disagreement and distress go underground. Deliberation surfaces the values in play, draws on everyone's knowledge of the client and lets the team own a considered judgment it can revisit.

title: Moral habituation
summary: Building a virtue such as courage or temperance by repeatedly doing what that virtue would do, in graded steps and with reflection after each attempt, until the right action and the right feelings come readily; in Aristotle's account, the main route by which character virtues are acquired.
selfCheck: What small act this week would be a genuine rung up the ladder for me, rather than a leap or no step at all?
Am I doing this because it is the right thing to do here, or mainly to look brave, generous or disciplined?
Did I reflect after the last attempt, or am I just repeating it by rote?
Does this kind of action feel easier or more satisfying than it did a month ago, and if not, is the step the right size?
Am I sliding past the mean into the opposite fault, such as rashness instead of courage?
steps: Name one virtue you want more of and the concrete situations where you currently fall short of it (for courage, perhaps raising concerns in meetings or declining unreasonable requests).
List those situations from mildest to hardest, and pick one at the bottom that is uncomfortable but clearly manageable.
Do the act on purpose, for the reason the virtue cares about, not for show; rehearse it first if it helps.
Afterwards, note what you did, how it felt, and how it landed, and adjust what you will do differently next time.
Repeat at the same level until it feels fairly easy and even satisfying, then move one rung up.
Check periodically with someone whose judgment you trust whether you are hitting the mean or drifting toward its excess, such as rashness or rigidity.

example.situation: A project coordinator notices that she agrees in meetings to deadlines she knows are unrealistic, then works late to cover the gap. She wants to become someone who says what she actually thinks.
example.before: She reads a book on assertiveness, resolves to be braver, and at the next big review abruptly tells a senior sponsor in front of everyone that the whole plan is unworkable, then retreats into silence for weeks after it goes badly.
example.after: She starts small: this week she asks one clarifying question about scope in her own team's stand-up; next week she proposes a realistic date for a minor task; later she flags a risk to her manager one to one. After each, she jots down what happened and what to tweak, and only takes on the sponsor review once the smaller acts feel natural.
example.why: Character changes through repeated, well-aimed acts rather than through resolutions or one dramatic leap. Graded practice with reflection builds both the habit and the judgment to use it at the right time and in the right measure.

title: Moral virtues
summary: Settled excellences of character, such as courage, temperance, generosity, justice and truthfulness, that dispose a person to feel and act well. Aristotle distinguished them from the intellectual virtues: they are acquired by habit rather than by teaching, and in their full form they cannot exist without practical wisdom.
selfCheck: Am I doing the right thing gladly, grudgingly, or only because I would be embarrassed not to?
Is my good impulse here being guided by judgment about this situation, or just by my usual temperament?
Would I act the same way if the setting changed, if I were rushed, unobserved or in a different mood?
Which of my virtues reliably show up at work but not at home, or the other way round?

example.situation: A team lead is generous by temperament. When a struggling colleague asks for a second extension on a deliverable that other people are waiting on, she feels the familiar pull to say yes again.
example.before: "Of course, take another week." She absorbs the extra work herself, the downstream team slips, and the colleague never hears that the pattern is a problem.
example.after: She asks what is actually blocking the work, offers a specific piece of help and a firm new date, and tells the downstream team plainly what has changed.
example.why: Kindness of temperament is what Aristotle would call natural virtue: a good starting point that can still misfire. It becomes a full virtue only when practical wisdom aims it at what genuinely helps everyone involved, at the right time and in the right way.

title: Morton Deutsch
summary: American social psychologist (1920–2017) who founded the modern study of conflict resolution: his theory of cooperation and competition and his account of constructive versus destructive conflict ask what turns a disagreement between people into a shared problem or a spiral of suspicion.

title: Mourning and Melancholia
summary: Sigmund Freud's short 1917 essay (written 1915) that compares ordinary mourning with melancholic depression and describes the "work of mourning", the slow, painful withdrawal of attachment from someone who has died. Often called the first major psychological theory of grief, it gave later grief theory both its starting point and its most criticised assumption: that healthy grief ends in letting go.

title: Negative visualization
summary: A Stoic exercise of deliberately imagining that you could lose what you value, or that a setback could happen, so that you hold good things with more appreciation and meet misfortune with less shock.
selfCheck: Am I rehearsing a possible loss in order to prepare and appreciate, or am I just worrying?
After imagining this loss, did I come back to what I still have and what I can do now?
Which parts of the outcome I fear are actually up to me?
steps: Choose one thing you value and tend to take for granted, such as a relationship, your health, your job or an ordinary comfort.
Remind yourself plainly of its nature, starting small, for example that this mug can break and that the people you love are mortal.
For a minute or two, imagine concretely what your life would be like without it, or how it might never have come about.
Return to the present and notice that you do still have it; name one way you will use or appreciate it today.
Before a risky plan, list what could go wrong, separate what is up to you from what is not, and prepare for the parts you can influence.
Stop if the exercise turns into dread or repetitive worry, and shorten it or set it aside.

example.situation: Your manager asks you to present to senior leadership next week, and you also have a job you mostly enjoy but have started to complain about.
example.before: I'll keep replaying how badly the presentation could go every night until then, and keep grumbling about this job.
example.after: Once, I'll list what could go wrong in the presentation, prepare for the questions I can foresee, and accept that the reaction isn't fully up to me. And I'll take a minute to picture not having this job at all, then notice what I'd miss.
example.why: A brief, bounded rehearsal turns vague fear into preparation and restores appreciation, whereas dwelling on the worst only adds suffering before anything has happened.

title: Personal and general wisdom
summary: Ursula Staudinger's distinction between general wisdom, insight into life and people in general (as when advising someone else), and personal wisdom, insight into one's own life; research finds the two related but distinct, with different correlates, age trajectories and ways of being trained.
selfCheck: Am I drawing on what I know about life in general here, or on what I actually know about myself in this situation?
If a friend described this exact problem to me, what would I tell them, and why am I not following that advice now?
What does this setback show me about my own strengths and weaknesses that I would rather not look at?
Am I calling myself wise about this because I give good advice to others, or because I have handled my own version of it well?

title: Perspective-taking
aliases: putting yourself in someone else's shoes
summary: Deliberately imagining a situation from another person's point of view, including what they know, want and feel, as a way to understand them and connect with them; best paired with simply asking them.
selfCheck: Am I imagining how they feel, or how I would feel in their place?
Which of my beliefs about their view have I actually checked with them?
Have I asked a question I don't already know the answer to?
Is there an option that meets what they want as well as what I want?
steps: Before you respond, name your own first reading of the situation so you can set it aside for a moment.
Imagine the other person's day, constraints and goals, and ask what they know that you don't and what they want from this.
Write down two or three guesses about how they see it, and mark each one as a guess.
Check the guesses by asking open questions ("How does this look from where you sit?") and listen without rebutting.
Revise your reading with what you heard, then decide what to do, looking for an option that serves both of you.

example.situation: A team lead notices that a usually reliable colleague has missed two deadlines in a row and seems curt in meetings.
example.before: I decide they've stopped caring, picture how I'd feel if I were slacking, and send a sharp message about accountability.
example.after: I sketch what their fortnight probably looked like, note that I'm guessing, then ask privately how the project is going from their side. It turns out a second project landed on them without my knowing; we reprioritise together.
example.why: Imagining their side softened my reaction, but only asking told me what was actually going on; taking and getting perspective together led to a fair and workable fix.

title: Post-traumatic growth
summary: Positive psychological change that people report after struggling with a highly challenging life event, such as deeper relationships, a stronger sense of personal strength or a greater appreciation of life. How often such reports reflect real change, rather than a hopeful story told afterwards, is disputed.

title: Practical wisdom
summary: The virtue, named phronesis by Aristotle and prudentia by medieval philosophers, of seeing what matters in a particular situation and working out well how to act on it for the good of oneself and others: good judgment about how to live, grown from experience and inseparable from good character.
selfCheck: What is the purpose behind the rule or plan I'm about to apply, and does applying it here actually serve that purpose?
Which particular features of this situation would an experienced, fair-minded person notice that I'm skating over?
Am I using my cleverness to reach a goal I haven't checked is worth reaching?
Whose interests, including my own, have I weighed, and whose have I quietly left out?
Have I asked someone with more experience of situations like this what they would see?

example.situation: A team lead's policy is that expense claims filed more than 30 days late are rejected. A reliable new hire files a claim six weeks late, after spending a month away dealing with a family emergency.
example.before: Rules are rules. If I make an exception for one person, I'll have to make it for everyone. Rejected.
example.after: "The rule exists to keep the books clean and stop sloppy filing, and neither is at stake here. I'll approve it, note the reason on the record, and suggest finance add a hardship clause so the next person isn't left to luck."
example.why: Practical wisdom serves the purpose behind a rule rather than its letter, notices what is particular about the case, and still protects fairness by making the reasoning visible and fixing the policy for everyone.

title: Process model of emotion regulation
aliases: extended process model of emotion regulation
summary: James Gross's map of where and how people can influence an emotion as it unfolds: by choosing or changing the situation, steering attention, rethinking what the situation means, or modulating the response once it has begun, together with the later decisions about whether to regulate, which strategy to use, and whether it is working.
selfCheck: Can I change this situation, or only how I see it and respond to it?
Am I reaching for my usual strategy, or the one that fits this moment?
Am I replaying this or concentrating on it, rather than rethinking it or looking elsewhere?
Is what I'm doing with this feeling working, or is it time to switch?
steps: When a strong feeling starts, name it and ask whether you actually want to change it, and in which direction.
Ask whether the situation itself can be avoided, chosen differently or changed; if it can, start there.
If the situation can't change, decide where to put your attention, and avoid dwelling on what upsets you.
Rethink what the situation means, for example by looking at it as a detached observer would.
Treat holding back your expression as a short-term tool for moments that need it, not a default.
After a few minutes, check whether the strategy is helping; keep it, switch, or stop.

example.situation: An employee opens an email, shortly before a client call, saying that a report they wrote has to be redone over the weekend.
example.before: Keep a straight face on the call, then spend the evening replaying the email and resenting it.
example.after: On the call, hold back the frustration since it's not the moment. Afterwards, ask the manager whether part of the work can wait until Monday. For the part that can't, look at it as an outsider would (a one-off, not a verdict on my work), then check an hour later whether that's actually settled the feeling or whether I need to talk it through.
example.why: The wiser response uses more than one point in the process (changing the situation where possible, reappraising what can't change, holding back only briefly) and checks whether the strategy is working instead of letting suppression slide into rumination.

title: Psychology of wisdom
summary: The branch of psychology and gerontology, active since the 1970s, that studies wisdom empirically: how ordinary people understand it, how to define and measure it, how it develops across the lifespan and varies between situations and cultures, and whether its components can be trained.

title: Purpose in life
summary: A lasting, central aim that organises a person's goals and daily choices, feels personally meaningful and, on most accounts, reaches beyond the self; psychologists treat it as one facet of meaning in life and a predictor, though not a proven cause, of better health and longer survival.

title: Regret
summary: The painful sense, on comparing what happened with what might have been, that a better outcome would have followed had you chosen differently; research finds it is the negative emotion people value most, and that it helps most when something can still be done and it is met with self-compassion rather than rumination.
selfCheck: Is there still something I can do about this, or is it time to let the goal go and invest in another?
Am I learning a specific lesson from this regret, or replaying the same scene and blaming myself?
Would I speak to a friend with this regret the way I am speaking to myself?
Which choice in front of me now am I most likely to regret not making?

example.situation: Two years ago you decided not to apply for a team-lead role; a colleague got it and is thriving, and the news of their promotion brings the old decision back.
example.before: I always bottle it. I keep replaying that week and telling myself what an idiot I was, or I insist I have no regrets at all and change the subject.
example.after: I did hold back, and I wish I hadn't. What was I afraid of, and is that still true? The next lead role opens in spring, so this month I'll ask my manager for a stretch project and say plainly that I want to be considered.
example.why: The wiser response accepts the regret without self-attack, extracts the lesson and turns it toward an opportunity that is still open, which is when regret is most useful.

title: Emotion regulatory flexibility
summary: The ability to fit how you handle a feeling to the situation you are in: reading what the moment calls for, having more than one way to respond (showing or holding back, rethinking or accepting), and noticing whether your chosen way is working so you can switch.
selfCheck: Does this moment call for showing what I feel, holding it back, or rethinking the situation?
Am I reaching for the strategy I always use, or the one that fits here?
Is the way I'm handling this feeling actually working, and if not, what else could I try?
Do I have at least two different ways to respond when something like this happens?

example.situation: A manager learns in a one-to-one that her team's project is being cancelled, and has to tell the team in an hour.
example.before: Whatever I feel, I keep it off my face. That's how I always handle bad news, at work and at home.
example.after: Stay composed while announcing it, since the team needs steadiness; then say plainly that she is disappointed too, ask how they're taking it, and later talk it through with a peer. If the composure starts to feel brittle, switch to rethinking what the cancellation frees the team to do.
example.why: Holding back expression was right for the announcement and wrong as a blanket rule; reading the moment, having more than one response, and checking whether it works is what the research links to better adjustment.

title: Resilience
summary: Keeping a fairly stable, healthy level of functioning through and after a loss, trauma or other major stressor, rather than breaking down and later recovering. Researchers treat it mainly as an outcome that many people show, not a fixed trait that a few people have; how common it is depends on how it is measured.

title: Richard S. Lazarus
summary: American psychologist (1922–2002) at the University of California, Berkeley, whose cognitive appraisal theory held that stress and emotion depend on how a person judges what an event means for their goals and well-being; his film experiments and his work with Susan Folkman on coping are the source of reappraisal as a named way of changing how one feels.

title: Right speech
summary: The third factor of the Buddhist Noble Eightfold Path: training yourself to abstain from lying, divisive talk, harsh words and idle chatter, and to say what is true and beneficial, at the right time and with goodwill, even when it is unwelcome.
selfCheck: Is what I am about to say true, as far as I actually know, or is it a guess or a convenient story?
Will saying it help them or the situation, or does it mainly serve my comfort, my image or my wish to be right?
Is this the right moment and the right tone for them to be able to hear it?
Am I holding back something true and useful only because saying it would be awkward for me?
Did anything I said today divide people, wound someone needlessly or pass on gossip, and is there something I should put right?
steps: Before saying anything that matters, ask first whether it is true as far as you actually know, and drop it if it is not, however pleasing it would be.
Ask next whether it is beneficial, meaning it will help the listener or the situation rather than only relieve your feelings or win the point.
If it is true and beneficial but unwelcome, do not swallow it; choose a time when the person can hear it, and plan to say it plainly and gently.
Check your motive and tone, and speak from goodwill rather than irritation, contempt or a wish to look good.
While you are speaking, notice whether the words are causing needless hurt, and stop, slow down or rephrase if they are.
Afterwards, review the conversation; if your words did harm, admit it to the person or a trusted friend and resolve to do better, and if they went well, note what helped.
Watch for the four habits the tradition names, lying, divisive talebearing, harsh words and idle chatter, especially in casual talk where they are easiest to miss.

example.situation: The evening before a colleague presents to senior leadership, they send you their slides and ask, "Is this ready?" The analysis is solid, but the cost figure on slide 6 rests on an assumption you know finance has already rejected.
example.before: "Looks great, you'll be fine!" Or, at 11 pm, a long message listing every weakness you can find, ending with a suggestion to rethink the whole thing.
example.after: The analysis is strong. One thing to fix before tomorrow: slide 6 uses last quarter's cost assumption, which finance dropped. Want ten minutes in the morning to swap in the new number? Everything else I'd leave as it is.
example.why: The first reply is pleasing but untrue and leaves them exposed; the second is true but harsh, badly timed and more about your critique than their success. The wiser reply is true, useful and timed so it can be acted on, and its goodwill is plain.

title: Robert J. Sternberg
summary: American psychologist (Yale, Tufts, Oklahoma State, Cornell) best known for his work on intelligence, creativity and love, who helped launch the psychology of wisdom by studying people's implicit theories of it and proposed the balance theory, which treats wisdom as using one's abilities for a common good.

title: Rumination
summary: The habit of repeatedly and passively turning over your distress, its causes and its consequences, without moving toward a solution or acceptance; it feels like thinking a problem through but tends to deepen low mood and stall action.
selfCheck: Has this round of thinking produced a new insight or a next step, or am I replaying the same scene?
Am I asking how to deal with this, or only why it happened and what it says about me?
What would I advise a friend in exactly this position, and can I take that advice tonight?
Have I tested the fear I keep circling, or only rehearsed it?

example.situation: In your annual review, your manager says your project updates are often late. That night you cannot stop thinking about it.
example.before: "Why do I always do this? What does she really think of me? I'm probably the weakest person on the team." Two hours later you are still replaying the meeting and have decided nothing.
example.after: "If a colleague told me this, I'd ask what exactly went wrong and what they'd do next. The last three updates slipped because I waited for complete data. I'll propose a short interim update every Friday and check that works for her." Then you put it down for the night.
example.why: Asking what happened and how to act, from a step back, turns the same worry into a plan, whereas asking why in a self-critical loop keeps the hurt fresh and leaves the problem untouched.

title: Samuel Lyman Atwood Marshall
summary: American journalist and Army combat historian (1900–1977) who pioneered the group "interview after combat", the model for the after-action review, and whose famous claim that only about one infantryman in four fired his weapon was later shown to rest on little or no systematic data.

title: Satisficing
summary: Choosing by first deciding what would count as good enough, then searching only until an option meets that standard, instead of trying to find and confirm the single best option.
selfCheck: Did I decide what "good enough" means before I started comparing, or am I letting each new option move the target?
Is this choice important and hard to undo enough to justify searching for the best, or would a good option serve just as well?
Have I set a limit on how many options or how much time I will spend?
Now that I have chosen, am I still checking what I gave up or what others picked?
steps: Before you look at any options, write down the few things the choice must achieve and the minimum each must reach; this is your "good enough" line.
Decide in advance how much search the choice deserves, such as a number of options, a deadline or a budget of hours, scaled to how much is at stake and how reversible it is.
Look at options one at a time and take the first that clears every line, rather than collecting the whole field to rank.
If nothing clears the line within your search budget, lower one standard deliberately; if many options clear it at once, raise one, and say which and why.
Once you have chosen, stop comparing; do not keep checking the options you passed up or what others chose.
Keep maximizing-style search for the rare choices where a better option is worth the extra effort and the decision is hard to undo.

example.situation: A team lead has to replace the team's project-tracking tool within a month, and dozens of products are available.
example.before: I'll trial every serious tool on the market, build a forty-row comparison sheet and keep reading reviews until I'm sure we have the best one.
example.after: We need four things: our existing workflows, a single sign-on, an export option and a price under our budget. I'll trial tools from the shortlist IT already approved, adopt the first one that meets all four, and stop shopping once it's in.
example.why: Fixing the standard before searching turns an endless comparison into a bounded task, and stopping after the choice spares the team the second-guessing that research links to looking for the best.

title: Seeking counsel
summary: Deliberately asking well-chosen people for their view before an important or uncertain decision, and then giving their advice real weight rather than only using it to confirm what you already think.
selfCheck: Did I ask people who know this kind of decision, or only people who would agree with me?
Did I ask without signalling the answer I wanted?
When the advice differed from my view, did I actually move, or did I explain it away?
Have I asked anyone who has already lived through this choice how it felt afterwards?
steps: Name the decision and decide whether it is important and uncertain enough to deserve outside counsel.
Write down your own current view and how confident you are, before you ask anyone.
Choose two or three advisers who know this kind of situation, including at least one who has lived through it and one likely to disagree with you.
Ask each one separately and personally, describe the problem without revealing your preferred answer, and ask what they would do and why.
Ask anyone who has already been through the same choice how it actually turned out and felt for them.
Compare their answers with your own and move your view meaningfully toward the advice where they know more or agree with each other, noting where and why you still differ.
Make the decision yourself, take responsibility for it, and later tell your advisers what you decided and how it went.

example.situation: A team lead has a job offer from a fast-growing start-up and must answer by Friday. They are excited and have already half-decided to accept.
example.before: I'll ask my best friend, who always backs me, mention the salary first, and take the yes as confirmation.
example.after: I'll write down my own answer first, then ask a former colleague who joined a start-up two years ago how it really went, and a mentor who tends to be cautious. I won't tell them which way I'm leaning, and I'll actually shift my view if they both raise the same worry.
example.why: Asking advisers who know the terrain, without steering them, gives the decision a second independent view and the lived experience of someone who has already been there, which people tend to undervalue.

title: Self-deception
summary: Coming to believe, and keeping on believing, something one would prefer to be true in the face of evidence that points the other way, because desire, fear or self-regard biases how one seeks out, weighs and remembers that evidence; it is a leading obstacle to self-knowledge and to judging one's own conduct honestly.
selfCheck: What evidence would change my mind here, and have I actually gone looking for it?
Am I holding the evidence that flatters me to the same standard as the evidence that doesn't?
Who would tell me plainly how this looks from the outside, and have I asked them?
If I turned out to be wrong about this, what would it cost me, and is that cost shaping what I see?

example.situation: Six months ago you championed a new onboarding process for your team. Completion rates are flat, and two team leads have told you that new hires find it confusing.
example.before: Those two never liked the change, and the numbers are just seasonal. It needs another quarter.
example.after: If a peer had launched this and showed me these numbers, what would I tell them? I'll write down now what result would mean it isn't working, and ask two people who weren't involved to go through the data with me.
example.why: The first response explains away each unwelcome fact on its own terms. The second fixes a standard before looking and borrows outside eyes, which makes it harder for a wish to steer how the evidence is read.

title: Self-distancing
summary: Reflecting on your own feelings and problems from the vantage point of an outside observer, for example by picturing the scene as a "fly on the wall" or by silently addressing yourself by name or as "you", so that you can understand a difficult experience without being swept back into it.
selfCheck: Am I reliving this from the inside, or looking at it as an observer would?
Would I give a friend in my position the advice I am about to follow?
Have I asked what I might not know and how the other person sees this?
Is this distance helping me understand the feeling, or helping me avoid it?
steps: Notice the signs that you are immersed in an upsetting experience, such as replaying the same scene, rehearsing the same sentence or feeling the original anger or shame rise again.
Shift your vantage point by picturing the scene from across the room, as a neutral observer would see it, with yourself as one of the people in it.
Talk to yourself silently using your own name or "you" instead of "I", for example "Why is Sam so stung by this?"
Ask what lies behind the feeling and what you might be missing, rather than recounting again what happened.
Widen the frame by asking how the other people involved might see it, and how the situation could change over the coming months.
Ask what you would advise a friend in exactly this position, then choose one concrete next step.
Stop if the distance is turning into a way of avoiding the feeling or the problem, and seek support if the distress persists.

example.situation: Late on a Friday, your manager leaves a blunt comment on your project report saying the analysis "misses the point", and you feel your weekend souring.
example.before: I can't believe I got this so wrong. I'll keep rereading that comment, write a defensive reply tonight and hit send.
example.after: Why is Jordan so rattled by one line? Jordan doesn't yet know what the manager meant by 'the point'. If a friend showed me this, I'd tell them to ask one clarifying question on Monday, not to send a reply at midnight.
example.why: Viewing the moment as an observer cools the sting enough to admit what you don't know and to consider the other person's view, which is the kind of reasoning people find easier about a friend's problem than their own.

title: Self-reflection
summary: The deliberate habit of turning attention to your own thoughts, feelings, motives and conduct in order to understand them and act better next time; done well, it is curious rather than anxious and ends in insight or a changed course, not in replaying the same worry.
selfCheck: Am I examining this out of curiosity about what happened, or out of fear about what it says about me?
Has this reflection produced an insight or a next step I can name in one sentence?
Have I looked at the situation from at least one perspective other than my own?
Is there someone who saw what happened whose view I should hear before I settle on a lesson?

example.situation: A product launch you led slipped by three weeks, and the team retrospective is tomorrow morning.
example.before: You spend the evening going over the delay again and again, asking what is wrong with you and what your director must think, and arrive at the meeting tired, defensive and with nothing new to say.
example.after: You set aside twenty minutes, write down what you expected, what actually happened and where the gap first appeared, notice that you had dismissed an early warning from a colleague, and bring one change you will make in how you handle risk flags on the next project.
example.why: Reflection driven by curiosity and aimed at a lesson produces insight you can act on, whereas anxious self-scrutiny replays the hurt without improving the next decision.

title: Servant leadership
summary: An approach to leading, named by Robert K. Greenleaf in 1970, in which the leader's first motive is to serve: attending to each follower's needs and growth as ends in themselves, holding people and resources in trust, and staying accountable to the wider community the organisation affects.
selfCheck: Are the people I lead growing - more capable, more independent - because of how I lead them?
Am I serving their real needs, or just pleasing them and avoiding hard calls?
Who outside my team, especially with the least power, is affected by this decision, and have I considered them?
Is serving others leaving me exhausted or torn between conflicting demands, and have I asked for the support I need?
steps: Before a decision that affects your team, write down who it serves and what each person directly affected needs from it.
Hold a regular one-to-one with each person that is about their growth (skills, goals, what is getting in their way), not only about tasks.
Remove one concrete obstacle per week that is slowing someone else down, and tell them it is done.
Persuade rather than order where time allows - explain the reasons for a decision and listen to objections before closing it.
Ask how the decision lands on people outside the team (customers, other departments, the community), and on the least powerful people it touches.
Keep setting direction and holding standards, and say no to requests that would serve one person at the cost of the team or the work.
Protect your own capacity - agree with your own manager what you can take on, and get support when serving others starts to drain you.

example.situation: A team lead is asked to move a capable junior analyst onto a high-visibility project that the lead could take on personally, and the analyst has said she wants to build client-facing skills.
example.before: I'll keep the client project myself - it's my chance to shine, and she can stay on the reporting work she's good at.
example.after: This project is the growth she asked for. I'll give it to her, sit in on the first two client calls, debrief her after each one, and make sure her name is on the result when we report upward.
example.why: The wiser response treats the analyst's development as a goal in its own right while still guarding the quality of the work, which is the balance servant leadership asks for; it also avoids using the role mainly to advance oneself.

title: Seven Sages of Greece
summary: An ancient Greek tradition, taking shape in the sixth and fifth centuries BCE, that honoured a changing list of seven practical sages of the archaic age (usually including Thales, Solon, Bias, Pittacus, Chilon and Cleobulus) and credited them with short maxims such as "Know thyself" and "Nothing in excess".

title: Socioemotional selectivity theory
summary: Laura Carstensen's lifespan theory that people's goals depend on how much time they feel they have left: when the future seems open, they favour exploration and new information; when it feels limited, they prioritise emotionally meaningful relationships and experiences.

title: Socratic ignorance
aliases: knowing that one does not know
summary: The teaching, drawn from Plato's Apology, that the beginning of human wisdom is not thinking you know what you do not know: an honest awareness of the limits of your own understanding, especially about the most important questions of how to live.
selfCheck: Do I actually know this, or am I only confident about it?
If someone questioned me closely here, where would my account run out?
Am I treating skill in my own field as if it made me an authority on this question too?

example.situation: A team lead is asked in a planning meeting whether a new supplier can deliver on time, and has only skimmed their proposal.
example.before: Yes, they're solid, I'm sure of it. Let's lock them in.
example.after: I've only skimmed it, so I don't actually know. Here's what I'd need to check, and who has worked with them before?
example.why: Separating what you know from what you merely feel sure of keeps a confident guess from becoming the team's decision, and invites the people who do know to speak.

title: Socratic philosophy
summary: The way of doing philosophy that began with Socrates of Athens (469–399 BCE) and was carried on by his followers: examining one's own and others' beliefs through questioning, admitting what one does not know, and treating care of the soul, meaning one's character and understanding, as more important than wealth or reputation.

title: Solomon's paradox
summary: The tendency to reason more wisely about other people's problems than about our own: people facing a friend's conflict more readily admit what they do not know, seek compromise, weigh other viewpoints and expect change than they do when the same conflict is theirs.
selfCheck: If a friend brought me this exact problem, what would I tell them, and am I following that advice myself?
Could I state the other person's view in words they would accept as fair?
Have I admitted what I don't know about their motives and about how this could unfold?
Am I treating any compromise as a defeat?

example.situation: You recently helped a teammate think calmly through a clash with another department. This week a peer quietly reassigns part of your own project without asking you.
example.before: This is a power grab, plain and simple. I know exactly what they're up to, and I'm escalating to our director today.
example.after: If my teammate described this to me, I'd ask what they actually know about the peer's reasons, what a fair split could look like, and how it might look in a month. I'll ask the peer for ten minutes first.
example.why: Treating your own conflict as you would a colleague's brings back the habits you already use as an adviser, namely admitting what you don't know, looking for compromise and expecting the situation to change.

title: Steven C. Hayes
summary: American clinical psychologist and behaviour analyst at the University of Nevada, Reno, who developed relational frame theory and, with colleagues, acceptance and commitment therapy (ACT), the source of cognitive defusion and of "psychological flexibility" as a goal; how strong ACT's evidence is compared with established therapies is still disputed.

title: Stewardship
summary: The disposition to treat a role, a team, an institution or a resource as something held in trust for others, putting the long-term good of the people it serves (including those who will come later) ahead of one's own short-term gain, and taking personal responsibility for leaving it in better shape than one found it.
selfCheck: If I handed this role, team or budget to someone tomorrow, would it be in better or worse shape than when I received it?
Who will live with the consequences of this decision after I have moved on, and have I counted their interests?
Am I taking responsibility for this outcome, or quietly protecting my own record?
Am I calling it stewardship when I am really keeping control that others should share?

example.situation: An engineering manager can hit this quarter's delivery target by skipping overdue maintenance on a system the team will hand over to another group next year.
example.before: Ship the features and skip the maintenance. The target is mine; the next team can deal with the debt.
example.after: Show my director what skipping the work would cost the team that inherits the system, propose a smaller feature set plus the essential fixes, and write a clear handover note either way.
example.why: The first response treats the system as a means to one person's quarterly result. The stewardly response treats it as held in trust for its future users and owners, accepts a visible short-term cost, and is honest with the people who set the target.

title: Stoicism
summary: A Hellenistic school of philosophy, founded in Athens around 300 BCE by Zeno of Citium, which teaches that virtue is the only true good and that a flourishing life comes from living in agreement with nature and reason, judging wisely what is and is not up to us.

title: Susan Nolen-Hoeksema
summary: American clinical psychologist (1959–2013) at Stanford, Michigan and Yale who developed response styles theory and showed how rumination, passively dwelling on distress, deepens and prolongs depression and helps explain why women are more often depressed than men.

title: Teaching for wisdom
summary: An approach to teaching, introduced by Robert Sternberg, that weaves wise thinking into ordinary subjects: learners work through real dilemmas, weigh their own, others' and wider interests over the short and long term, take opposing viewpoints seriously and reflect on their values, so that they learn how to use what they know and not just what to know.
selfCheck: When I explained this to someone, did I only hand over the right answer, or did I ask whose interests are at stake and over what time span?
Did I let the other person argue a view I disagree with, from that side, before I judged it?
Did I show that I can be wrong, or did I present myself as the one who always knows?
Which did I reward, the quick and clever answer or the balanced one?
steps: Pick a real dilemma from material you already teach (a historical episode, a case, a customer complaint) in which people's interests genuinely conflict.
Have learners list whose interests are at stake (their own, other people's, the wider community's) and what each option does to them in the short and the long run.
Ask each learner to argue the strongest case for a view they reject, from inside that person's position, then to look for a resolution that takes both sides into account.
Ask them to name the values behind their choice and to judge whether the means are acceptable, not only the result.
Lay out the three moves open to them (adapt to the situation, change it, or leave it) and have them say which fits best and why.
Model the habits yourself by saying what you don't know, changing your mind in front of them when given a good reason, and sharing credit.
Grade or praise answers for how well they balance interests and perspectives, then close by asking where a similar choice shows up in learners' own lives.

example.situation: A manager is training new shift supervisors. The case for the day: two staff members both asked for the same holiday weekend off, and only one can be released.
example.before: The manager explains the leave policy (first to ask gets priority), confirms that the trainees can recite it, and moves on to the next slide.
example.after: The manager has the trainees list everyone affected (both employees, the rest of the team, customers), what each option means this month and next year, and the best case for the person who would lose out. They discuss whether the rule should simply be applied, bent or changed, and the manager describes a time they handled a similar request badly and what they learned.
example.why: Knowing the rule is not the same as judging well when it collides with people's real interests; practising that judgment on the job's actual content builds the habit the trainees will need on the floor.

title: Temperance
summary: The character trait of wanting and enjoying bodily pleasures such as food, drink and sex in the right amount, at the right time and in the right way, so that appetite agrees with good judgment rather than fighting it; in Aristotle's account it is a mean between self-indulgence and a rare insensibility to pleasure.
selfCheck: Am I choosing this pleasure, or is habit or the people around me choosing it for me?
Will I still be glad of this amount tomorrow, given what I need to do and who depends on me?
Am I treating every pleasure as suspect, mistaking joylessness for discipline?
Where could I change my surroundings so I meet this temptation less often, instead of relying on resisting it?

example.situation: The night before you present to a client, your team takes them to dinner with an open bar. Colleagues are ordering round after round.
example.before: Either keep pace with the table so you don't look stiff, or refuse everything and sit through the evening tense and joyless.
example.after: Enjoy the meal and a drink with the group, switch to water when the rounds speed up, and leave at a sensible hour with a friendly word to the host.
example.why: Matching the table hands your judgment to the room, and grim refusal mistakes temperance for having no pleasure at all. The temperate response enjoys what fits the occasion while keeping tomorrow's aim in view, which is what Aristotle means by desiring what one ought, as and when one ought.

title: Theoretical wisdom
summary: The kind of wisdom Aristotle called sophia: deep understanding of the most fundamental and highest things, joining grasp of first principles with knowledge of what follows from them, prized for its own sake rather than for use, and distinguished from practical wisdom (phronesis), which is good judgment about how to act.

title: The Theory of Moral Sentiments
summary: Adam Smith's first book (1759; sixth, much-revised edition 1790), which explains moral judgment through sympathy, our imaginative placing of ourselves in another's situation, and through the "impartial spectator", an imagined fair observer we learn to consult when judging our own conduct.

title: Three-dimensional model of wisdom
summary: Monika Ardelt's model of personal wisdom as the integration of three personality qualities: a cognitive desire to understand life deeply, a reflective habit of seeing events and oneself from many perspectives, and compassionate concern for others; it is measured by the self-report Three-Dimensional Wisdom Scale (3D-WS).
selfCheck: Am I trying to understand what is really going on here, including what I cannot know, or only looking for facts that confirm my first reaction?
Have I looked at this situation, and my own part in it, from at least one other person's point of view?
Is my response moved by concern for the people affected, or mainly by protecting my ego?

title: Ubuntu
summary: A southern African ethical tradition, named by the Nguni word for "humanness", which holds that a person becomes fully human through relationships with others, and that a good life is one of identity with and solidarity towards a community.

title: The view from above
summary: A Stoic reflective exercise of imagining yourself raised high above the earth, and stretched across time, so that a present worry, ambition or grievance is seen at its true scale within the whole of human life.
selfCheck: Seen from far above and years from now, how big is this, really?
Am I using the wider view to act better here, or to stop caring about people who are affected?
Which part of this is about my reputation, and which part is about what is right to do?
steps: Name the specific thing that is gripping you right now, such as a slight, a setback, a rivalry or a wish for praise.
Picture yourself rising slowly above the room, the building and the city until you can see whole countries and the many lives going on in them at once.
Widen the view in time as well, recalling the people who lived before you and those who will come after, few of whom will ever know of this moment.
From that height, look back at your situation and ask how large it really is, and what part of it actually depends on you.
Come back down deliberately and choose one concrete, decent action for today, so the wider view ends in conduct rather than detachment.
Stop and set the exercise aside if it leaves you feeling that nothing matters, and talk to someone you trust instead.

example.situation: A colleague's proposal is chosen over yours in front of the whole department, and you spend the evening composing a sharp reply-all email.
example.before: Everyone saw that. I'm sending this tonight so they know the decision was wrong and I won't be pushed aside.
example.after: Picture this from far above: one meeting among millions happening today, which few will remember next year. What matters is the project and how I treat people. I'll sleep on it, then ask my manager what would have made my proposal stronger.
example.why: Seeing the slight at its real scale lowers the heat of the moment, and coming back down to one useful action keeps the wider view from turning into either revenge or indifference.

title: Viktor E. Frankl
summary: Viennese neurologist and psychiatrist (1905–1997), Holocaust survivor and founder of logotherapy, whose account of the camps, Man's Search for Meaning, made the search for meaning a central idea in modern psychology and in popular thinking about how to live through suffering; historians and later research have questioned parts of his account and theory.

title: Virtue ethics
summary: An approach to ethics that puts character at the centre: instead of starting from duties or outcomes, it asks what a good person is like and how to live well, treating virtues such as honesty, courage and practical wisdom as excellent, settled traits that shape how we see, feel, choose and act.

title: Vivian Clayton
summary: American psychologist, later a geriatric neuropsychologist in California, whose 1970s graduate research is credited as the first attempt to study wisdom empirically; with James Birren she described wisdom as joining cognitive, reflective and affective (compassionate) qualities, and she distinguished wisdom, as judgment about whether to act, from intelligence, as skill at how to act.

title: Weakness of will
summary: Freely and knowingly doing something other than what you yourself judge best, or abandoning a resolution you had good reason to keep. Aristotle's name for it, akrasia, marks the gap between knowing what is wise and doing it, a gap that practical wisdom has to close.
selfCheck: Am I changing my plan because I have learned something new, or only because the moment of keeping it has arrived?
If I asked myself yesterday, when I made this resolution, would I accept the reason I am now giving for dropping it?
What is the specific cue that usually pulls me off course here, and have I planned what I will do when it appears?
Am I telling myself a story that makes the easier option look like the wiser one?

example.situation: You decided on Sunday, for good reasons, to finish a grant report before answering the week's routine email. On Monday morning the inbox shows forty unread messages.
example.before: "I'll just clear these quickly so my head is free, then start the report." By lunch the report is untouched, and you tell yourself that answering email was the responsible choice after all.
example.after: "When I sit down at nine, I open the report file before the inbox." You close the mail app, work for ninety minutes, and then deal with email in a block you had already scheduled.
example.why: The first response quietly rewrites a sound resolution at the moment temptation is strongest. The second decides in advance when and where the better judgment will be acted on, and removes the cue that would trigger the lapse.

title: Wisdom
summary: Doing well, in thought and in action, with respect to how to live: knowing or reasonably believing what matters, seeing the limits of what one knows, and using that understanding to judge, advise and act well. Philosophers debate its exact conditions; psychologists describe it as morally grounded metacognition applied to real problems.
selfCheck: Am I treating how much I know about this as if it were the same as knowing what to do?
What in this situation am I unsure of, and have I admitted it to myself and to others?
Would this choice still look good to me if I judged it by the kind of life I want to live, not only by today's goal?

example.situation: A team member with deep technical knowledge is asked whether the team should rebuild a struggling product from scratch or keep repairing it.
example.before: I know this codebase better than anyone, so the answer is obviously a rewrite. No need to hear the others.
example.after: I know the code well, but not the customers' timelines or the budget. Let me lay out what I'm sure of and what I'm guessing, ask sales and finance what I'm missing, and recommend the option that serves the people who depend on this, not the one I'd enjoy.
example.why: Expertise is not yet wisdom; the wiser answer knows the limits of its own knowledge, takes other perspectives in, and aims at the good of everyone affected.

title: Wisdom and well-being
summary: The observed, modest and uneven association between wisdom and well-being: people who score high on wisdom tend to report good lives, but many people are satisfied without being especially wise, and the link depends heavily on how wisdom and well-being are measured.

title: Wisdom in the professions
summary: The situation of a doctor, teacher, lawyer, nurse, manager or any other worker whose job serves other people and regularly presents cases that rules, scripts, targets and incentives do not fit, so that doing the work well depends on judging what this case calls for and wanting to serve the purpose the job exists for.
selfCheck: What is this job for, and would the people it serves recognise what I am about to do as serving that purpose?
Is this a case the rule was written for, or one its authors did not foresee?
Am I departing from the protocol because the case demands it, or because it is inconvenient or I am overconfident?
Am I doing this because it is right for the person in front of me, or because it moves the number I am paid on?
Who could I talk this case through with before acting, and will I report the misfit so the rule can improve?

example.situation: A customer-support agent is measured on call length. A distressed caller has been wrongly billed for months and is clearly confused by the standard explanation the script provides.
example.before: Read the scripted answer, open a ticket, and end the call inside the six-minute target. The metric is what my review looks at.
example.after: Take the extra few minutes to understand what went wrong, explain it in plain terms, and fix or escalate it properly; afterwards, tell my team lead the script failed this case and suggest how to change it.
example.why: The script and the target exist to serve customers, so following them against that purpose gets the letter right and the job wrong. The wiser agent also treats the misfit as information for the system, rather than quietly working around it every time.

title: Wise leadership
summary: Leading with practical wisdom: judging what is good for the organisation and for the people and society it affects, seeing the particulars of a situation clearly, handling uncertainty openly, and turning that judgment into action and into the judgment of others.
selfCheck: Whose interests does this decision touch, and have I weighed them or only the ones I'm measured on?
What do I not know here, and have I said so to the people relying on me?
Is my confidence coming from the facts of this case, or from my position and past success?
What will the people who watched me decide this learn about how to decide?

example.situation: A team lead is told to ship a feature by Friday to hit a quarterly target; testing has found that it occasionally shows one customer's order history to another.
example.before: Ship it. The bug is rare, the target is mine, and we'll patch it quietly next sprint.
example.after: Lay out who is affected (customers, the support team, the company's reputation, the people chasing the target), tell my manager plainly what we know and don't know about the bug, propose shipping without the faulty part, and walk the junior engineer who found it through how I'm weighing it.
example.why: The wiser response weighs everyone the decision touches rather than one metric, is honest about uncertainty, and uses the moment to build someone else's judgment.

title: Wise reasoning
summary: A measurable way of thinking through uncertain, conflict-laden problems that combines intellectual humility, attention to other people's perspectives, recognition that situations can change and unfold in several ways, and a search for compromise or integration of viewpoints.
selfCheck: What don't I know about this situation, and how sure am I really about the other person's motives?
Could I describe the other side's view in words they would accept as fair?
How might this look in a month or a year, and what else could happen besides the outcome I fear?
Is there an arrangement that meets the main concerns on both sides, or am I treating any middle ground as losing?
Would I reason about this differently if a friend had brought it to me?

example.situation: Your team lead announces that a project you have run for a year will be merged into another group's work. You learn about it in the same meeting as everyone else.
example.before: They have clearly sidelined me on purpose. I'll tell the team the plan is a mistake and refuse to hand anything over.
example.after: I don't yet know why this was decided or who pushed for it. I'll ask the lead what problem the merger solves, say plainly what I think would be lost, and propose a handover that keeps the parts that work. This may look different in three months.
example.why: The wiser response admits what it does not know, takes the other side's reasons seriously, allows that events can still turn several ways, and looks for an arrangement both sides can live with, which are the four elements researchers score.
